entries.question: How do I join a team in RackTrack?
entries.answer: You can join a team by either creating a new organization and waiting for approval, or by accepting an invitation link from an existing organization. If you're creating a new organization, you'll need to provide details such as email, username, organization name, and a strong password, and then verify your email address with a 6-digit code. If you're accepting an invitation, you'll need to open the invite link, choose a username and password, and join the organization.

entries.question: What happens after I create a new organization?
entries.answer: After you create a new organization, you'll need to wait for approval from the platform owner. You'll be taken to a waiting room where you'll see a message indicating that your organization is pending approval. Once your organization is approved, you'll be able to access the app.

entries.question: How do I recover my password if I'm locked out?
entries.answer: If you're locked out, you can use the Forgot Password feature to recover your access. You'll receive a one-minute code via email, which you can use to reset your password or sign in.

entries.question: What is the difference between a founder and an invitee?
entries.answer: A founder is someone who creates a new organization, while an invitee is someone who joins an existing organization through an invitation link. Founders need to wait for approval, while invitees can join immediately.

entries.question: How do I know if my organization is approved?
entries.answer: You'll receive a message in the waiting room indicating whether your organization is pending, rejected, or deactivated. If your organization is approved, you'll be able to access the app.

entries.question: Can I choose my own role in the organization?
entries.answer: No, your role is determined by the account and is enforced on the server. You'll be routed to the correct screen based on your role when you sign in.

entries.question: What happens if I enter an incorrect password?
entries.answer: If you enter an incorrect password, you'll be prompted to try again. If you're still having trouble, you can use the Forgot Password feature to recover your access.

entries.question: Is my password stored securely?
entries.answer: Yes, your password is never stored in the clear. Reset codes are also short-lived and single-purpose, and are emailed to you securely.

entries.question: What is the role hierarchy in RackTrack?
entries.answer: The role hierarchy in RackTrack is owner, org admin, site manager, and member. Roles are enforced on the server and determine the level of access you have to the app.

entries.question: What happens if the probe fails?
entries.answer: If the probe fails, you can read the reason for the failure and press Retry to try again.

entries.question: How does the feature determine if a port is available or in use?
entries.answer: The feature determines if a port is available or in use by parsing the interface table from the switch. A port is considered available if it is link down and has no description, and in use if it is link up or connected.
symptoms: How does it know if a port is available?

entries.question: What is the difference between a reserved port and an available port?
entries.answer: A reserved port is a port that is administratively down, shut, or err-disabled, or a down port that still has a description. An available port is a port that is link down and has no description. Reserved ports do not count as open capacity.

entries.question: How does the feature classify ports as copper or fiber?
entries.answer: The feature classifies ports as copper or fiber by using the switch's medium column, or by inferring from the interface naming or the scan's SFP-cage count.
symptoms: How does it know if a port is copper or fiber?

entries.question: What is the utilization bar and what does it show?
entries.answer: The utilization bar shows the used capacity of the switch as a percentage of the total capacity.

entries.question: Can I use the Live Switch Data feature to plan a patch?
entries.answer: Yes, you can use the Live Switch Data feature to plan a patch by confirming a free copper port and its interface name before running a cable.
symptoms: How do I plan a patch?

entries.question: Can I use the Live Switch Data feature to check the capacity of a switch?
entries.answer: Yes, you can use the Live Switch Data feature to check the capacity of a switch by looking at the utilization bar, which shows at a glance whether a switch is nearly full.
symptoms: How do I check the capacity of a switch?

entries.question: How do I spot reserved ports using the Live Switch Data feature?
entries.answer: You can spot reserved ports using the Live Switch Data feature by using the Errors filter, which reveals ports that are down on purpose.
symptoms: How do I spot reserved ports?

entries.question: What is the purpose of the CMDB Registration & Reconciliation feature in RackTrack?
entries.answer: The CMDB Registration & Reconciliation feature in RackTrack is used to register the devices, ports, and connections in a rack into the CMDB and to reconcile any discrepancies between the physical rack and the CMDB records. It raises alerts and creates work notes or tickets for any mismatches found.
symptoms: CMDB expects vs scan sees at U##

entries.question: How do I register a new rack in RackTrack?
entries.answer: To register a new rack in RackTrack, you need to perform a fresh scan of the unregistered rack. An approval card will appear, and you can choose to 'Raise Ticket' and then 'Approve' to synchronize the inventory. You will see a 'Successfully registered' summary with counts and a device list.

entries.question: What happens when a discrepancy is found between the physical rack and the CMDB records?
entries.answer: When a discrepancy is found between the physical rack and the CMDB records, a 'Physical Drift Detected' alert appears. You can use the 'Raise ticket' action to open an incident inline for the drift, and a work note or ticket will be posted to the actual incident/CMDB backend.
symptoms: CMDB expects vs scan sees at U##

entries.question: What is the difference between real and synthetic data in the CMDB Registration & Reconciliation feature?
entries.answer: The registered device list and counts are real data, coming from the scan's detected inventory. Some connection and asset fields are synthetic, meaning they are placeholder values mixed into the push. Reconciliation verdicts are real, computed from expected-class-at-U vs detected-class-at-U.

entries.question: Can I use the CMDB Registration & Reconciliation feature to onboard a new rack?
entries.answer: Yes, the CMDB Registration & Reconciliation feature can be used to onboard a new rack. A single scan can register the whole rack's inventory into the CMDB via a guided approval.

entries.question: How does the CMDB Registration & Reconciliation feature handle duplicate tickets?
entries.answer: The CMDB Registration & Reconciliation feature uses a stable hash to compare the scan vs records and produces a content hash. If the hash is unchanged, no duplicate tickets are raised. If the hash is changed, a note is appended instead.

entries.question: What is the purpose of the 'Raise ticket' action in the CMDB Registration & Reconciliation feature?
entries.answer: The 'Raise ticket' action is used to open an incident inline for a drift detected between the physical rack and the CMDB records. It allows you to create a work note or ticket for the discrepancy found.

entries.question: Can I use the CMDB Registration & Reconciliation feature to prove physical drift?
entries.answer: Yes, the CMDB Registration & Reconciliation feature can be used to prove physical drift. A ticket-linked scan can show that a device is at the wrong unit or missing, and raise it with evidence.

entries.question: What is the purpose of the Connections & Integrations feature in RackTrack?
entries.answer: The Connections & Integrations feature allows you to manage external systems that RackTrack pulls data from, such as ServiceNow, NetBox, and Orion. You can add connections, store credentials securely, and make one connection active at a time to drive the data shown on the screens.
symptoms: No data is being pulled from external sources

entries.question: How do I add a new connection in RackTrack?
entries.answer: To add a new connection, press the 'Add connection' button and enter a name, type, and the type-specific credential fields. The credentials will be encrypted and stored securely, and you can then make the connection active to drive the data shown on the screens.

entries.question: What happens when I make a connection active in RackTrack?
entries.answer: When you make a connection active, it drives the data shown on every screen in the app. You can only have one active connection at a time, and making a new connection active will refresh the downstream data.
symptoms: Data is not updating after making a new connection active

entries.question: How do I refresh the data from an active connection in RackTrack?
entries.answer: To refresh the data from an active connection, press the 'Refresh data' button. This will pull fresh records from the source and update the data shown on the screens.

entries.question: What happens to my credentials when I add a new connection in RackTrack?
entries.answer: When you add a new connection, your credentials are encrypted and stored securely. They are never sent back to the client and are never displayed on the screen. If you need to edit the credentials, you will need to re-enter the secret to replace it.

entries.question: Can I have multiple active connections in RackTrack at the same time?
entries.answer: No, you can only have one active connection at a time in RackTrack. This ensures that there is a single, unambiguous source of truth behind every screen.

entries.question: Who can use the Connections & Integrations feature in RackTrack?
entries.answer: The Connections & Integrations feature is available to owners and organization admins. They can add connections, make them active, and manage the credentials securely.

entries.question: What is the purpose of the 'Use' button on a connection in RackTrack?
entries.answer: The 'Use' button on a connection allows you to make that connection active. This will drive the data shown on every screen in the app and refresh the downstream data.

entries.question: How do I rotate credentials for a connection in RackTrack?
entries.answer: To rotate credentials for a connection, you need to re-enter the secret to replace it. This ensures that the old credentials are never exposed and the new credentials are encrypted and stored securely.

entries.question: What does the Firmware Check feature do?
entries.answer: The Firmware Check feature tells you whether your device's firmware is up to date, what the latest version is, and what changes have been made in the latest release. It provides a plain-English verdict and release-note excerpts.

entries.question: How do I use the Firmware Check feature?
entries.answer: To use the Firmware Check feature, enter the make, model, and current version of your device. Then, press the 'Check firmware' button. The feature will compare your current version to the latest version and provide a verdict and release-note excerpts.

entries.question: What information do I need to provide to use the Firmware Check feature?
entries.answer: You need to provide the make, model, and current version of your device to use the Firmware Check feature. The make and model fields have type-ahead suggestions, and the current version field is free text.

entries.question: What kind of output does the Firmware Check feature provide?
entries.answer: The Firmware Check feature provides a verdict card with a colored headline and a plain-English body, a version-status card with a comparison pill, and release-note excerpts. It also provides fallback links to vendor support and web searches when data is thin.

entries.question: What happens if the Firmware Check feature cannot confirm the latest version?
entries.answer: If the Firmware Check feature cannot confirm the latest version, it will display a message indicating that the latest version cannot be confirmed and provide search links to vendor support and web searches.

entries.question: How does the Firmware Check feature prioritize upgrades?
entries.answer: The Firmware Check feature helps prioritize upgrades by providing a verdict and release-note excerpts. If a device is several releases behind, it will rise up the maintenance list.

entries.question: Can I use the Firmware Check feature for change planning?
entries.answer: Yes, the Firmware Check feature can be used for change planning. The release-note excerpts provide information on what changes have been made in the latest version, helping you plan for upgrades.

entries.question: What is the RackTrack Marketplace?
entries.answer: The RackTrack Marketplace is a place where users can buy, sell, or swap surplus networking and datacenter gear. It allows users to list surplus hardware for sale, post 'wanted' ads, or jump out to partner marketplaces with a pre-filled search.

entries.question: Who can use the Marketplace?
entries.answer: Everyone can browse the Marketplace, but posting and managing listings requires a sign-in. Signed-in users can post and manage their own listings.

entries.question: How do I browse listings on the Marketplace?
entries.answer: You can browse public listings by filtering by keyword, category, and for-sale/wanted. You can also open a listing card for full detail.

entries.question: How do I sell something on the Marketplace?
entries.answer: To sell something, you need to sign in and press the 'Sell something' button. You can publish a listing, which can be pre-filled from a scan result. You can manage your own listings by marking them as sold, reactivating, or deleting them.

entries.question: What information is required to create a listing?
entries.answer: To create a listing, you need to provide title, category, condition, optional vendor/model, price, quantity, location, a photo, and a description.

entries.question: Can I use a scan result to pre-fill a listing?
entries.answer: Yes, you can use a scan result to pre-fill a listing. The scan result can provide vendor/model/category/rack ID, which can be used to pre-fill the listing fields.

entries.question: What happens when I use the partner search bar?
entries.answer: When you use the partner search bar, you will be taken to a pre-filled search on a third-party site, such as eBay, Amazon, FS.com, or Curvature. No listing is created on the third-party site, and no data is exchanged beyond the query text.

entries.question: Are the listings on the Marketplace real or synthetic?
entries.answer: The listings on the Marketplace are real, posted by users. There is no demo seed data, and uploaded photos are also real.

entries.question: What are some common use cases for the Marketplace?
entries.answer: Some common use cases for the Marketplace include offloading surplus hardware, sourcing a replacement part, and finding a specific device. You can use the 'Sell this' action on a scan result to pre-fill a listing for the exact device, or post a wanted ad to find a replacement transceiver quickly.

entries.question: How do I manage my listings on the Marketplace?
entries.answer: You can manage your listings by signing in and accessing the 'My listings' view. From there, you can mark listings as sold, reactivate, or delete them.

entries.question: What is the multi-rack scan feature in RackTrack?
entries.answer: The multi-rack scan feature in RackTrack allows you to scan multiple racks at once by panning a video across several racks or uploading photos of each rack. It then splits the video or photos into individual racks, analyzes each one, and groups them together so you can view the entire row in 3D.

entries.question: How do I use the multi-rack scan feature?
entries.answer: To use the multi-rack scan feature, record a slow pan across the aisle or upload a photo per rack. The feature will then split the video or photos into individual racks, analyze each one, and group them together.

entries.question: What is the output of the multi-rack scan feature?
entries.answer: The output of the multi-rack scan feature is a rack group, where each rack is analyzed individually and grouped together with a combined 3D view. You can also view each rack individually and switch between them using the rack tabs.

entries.question: How does the multi-rack scan feature detect rack boundaries?
entries.answer: The multi-rack scan feature detects rack boundaries by looking for big horizontal shifts, scene-color changes, or detection-less blurry frames in the video or photos.

entries.question: What happens if the multi-rack scan feature fails to detect rack boundaries?
entries.answer: If the multi-rack scan feature fails to detect rack boundaries, it will treat the entire video or set of photos as a single rack.

entries.question: Can I use the multi-rack scan feature with synthetic data?
entries.answer: No, the multi-rack scan feature uses real data from your video or photos to analyze and group the racks. However, the combined-view cabling is synthetic, meaning it is inferred from the individual rack analyses.

entries.question: What are some common use cases for the multi-rack scan feature?
entries.answer: Some common use cases for the multi-rack scan feature include surveying a row of racks and reviewing the entire row in 3D for a layout overview.

entries.question: How does the multi-rack scan feature handle per-rack frames?
entries.answer: The multi-rack scan feature chooses the best frame per segment based on a weighted score of device count, mean confidence, and sharpness.

entries.question: What is the purpose of the rack tabs in the multi-rack scan feature?
entries.answer: The rack tabs in the multi-rack scan feature allow you to switch between individual racks and preserve the current sub-page when you switch racks.

entries.question: Can I use the multi-rack scan feature to view a specific rack's details?
entries.answer: Yes, you can use the quick-jump chips to open a specific rack's detail from the combined view.

entries.question: What does the Network View feature in RackTrack do?
entries.answer: The Network View feature joins your scanned rack to live network-discovery data to show real port up/down state, VLANs, LLDP/CDP neighbors, and how many MAC addresses each port has learned. It also lets you look up where any MAC ended up across the network.

entries.question: How do I use the Network View feature?
entries.answer: To use the Network View feature, open the Network View, read the match summary, expand a device card to load its port table, filter ports by Live/Up/Down/All, and click a learned-MAC count to look up where that address lives.

entries.question: What is the source of the data in the Network View?
entries.answer: The data in the Network View comes from live network discovery of the actual devices, matched to the scan. It is not synthesized or based on the scan or wiring.

entries.question: What information can I find in the device cards?
entries.answer: The device cards show the device's identity, IP, a ports-up bar, and a link count. They also show the device's name, class, model/vendor, and IP, and are dimmed if not discovered.

entries.question: How do I find an endpoint using the Network View?
entries.answer: To find an endpoint, use the MAC lookup feature. It reveals which port a device is learned behind, across the network.

entries.question: What is the difference between the Network View and the topology view?
entries.answer: The Network View shows logical, discovered connectivity, while the topology view shows physical layout with inferred cabling.

entries.question: Can I use the Network View to confirm if a link is really up?
entries.answer: Yes, the Network View shows the true operational state of the link, independent of the photo.

entries.question: What happens if the discovery database is not connected?
entries.answer: If the discovery database is not connected, the Network View will show a 'being prepared' message instead of raw errors.

entries.question: Can I seed the discovery database with a demo fabric for demonstration purposes?
entries.answer: Yes, the discovery database can be populated with a seeded demo fabric for demonstration. When real discovery is connected, the same view shows genuine live telemetry.

entries.question: How does the Network View handle bidirectional neighbors?
entries.answer: The Network View represents links in both directions, so they show consistently from either end.

entries.question: What is the Organization Administration feature in RackTrack?
entries.answer: The Organization Administration feature is a role-aware console that allows platform owners and organization admins to manage organizations, sites, members, and invitations. The owner can create, approve, rename, deactivate, or remove organizations, while an organization admin can manage their own org's sites, members, and integrations.

entries.question: Who can use the Organization Administration feature?
entries.answer: The Organization Administration feature can only be used by the platform owner and organization admins. Members and site managers are redirected away from the console.

entries.question: How do I open the Organization Administration console?
entries.answer: You can open the Organization Administration console from the Profile admin shortcut. The owner or admin scope will determine what you can do in the console.

entries.question: What can the platform owner do in the Organization Administration console?
entries.answer: The platform owner can view platform stats, create, approve, rename, deactivate, or remove organizations, and drill into any organization to see its sites, members, and scans.

entries.question: What can an organization admin do in the Organization Administration console?
entries.answer: An organization admin can add sites, add or edit members, set org-wide integrations, generate single-use invite links, and filter scan activity by person or site.

entries.question: How do I invite new members to an organization?
entries.answer: You can generate a single-use invite link from the Organization Administration console. The link is valid for 7 days and binds the new account to the invited org, site, and role.

entries.question: What happens when an organization is deactivated?
entries.answer: When an organization is deactivated, scanning is paused for all its members. The organization's admin will see a notice indicating that the organization is awaiting approval.

entries.question: Can I manage another organization admin's account?
entries.answer: No, one organization admin cannot manage another organization admin's account. The owner role can never be managed by others.

entries.question: What happens to a member's past scans when their account is removed?
entries.answer: When a member's account is removed, their past scans are preserved and kept on record.

entries.question: How do I filter scan activity by person or site?
entries.answer: You can filter scan activity by person or site from the Organization Administration console. Select a person or site to scope the scan grid.

entries.question: What is the Port History & Drift feature in RackTrack?
entries.answer: The Port History & Drift feature records every port change over time for a continuously monitored switch, including link up/down, speed, duplex, admin state, medium, description, and neighbor, to help spot re-cabling and flapping links.

entries.question: How often does the background poller check the switch for changes?
entries.answer: The background poller checks the switch about once a minute.

entries.question: What information is stored in the per-port timeline?
entries.answer: The per-port timeline stores colored segments for each period a value held, providing a visual representation of changes over time.

entries.question: How do I access the detail sheet for a specific port?
entries.answer: To access the detail sheet for a specific port, tap on the port in the interface grid.

entries.question: What is the purpose of the 'Value at' table?
entries.answer: The 'Value at' table shows the value that held at each time offset, providing a detailed view of changes over time.

entries.question: How does the system detect changes in neighbor information?
entries.answer: The system detects changes in neighbor information by tracking LLDP neighbor changes and displaying a color change on the timeline to flag re-cabling.

entries.question: What is the purpose of the change log?
entries.answer: The change log provides a human-readable record of events, including from→to values and timestamps, to help identify changes and issues.

entries.question: How do I use the Port History & Drift feature to chase a flapping link?
entries.answer: To chase a flapping link, use the change log to pinpoint exactly when a port went down and came back, and then investigate the cause of the issue.

entries.question: What is the purpose of the 'Poll now' button?
entries.answer: The 'Poll now' button allows you to manually poll the switch for updates, in addition to the automatic polling that occurs about once a minute.

entries.question: How does the system handle sparse early history?
entries.answer: The system expects sparse early history and accrues history only as the poller runs, providing a clear indication of when data is available.

entries.question: What does the Profile & Scan History feature do?
entries.answer: The Profile & Scan History feature shows who you are signed in as, your organization, and your most recent rack scans. You can tap any scan to reopen its full report. Admins and owners also get shortcuts to their management tools here.

entries.question: How do I access my profile and scan history?
entries.answer: You can access your profile and scan history by opening the Profile section from the bottom navigation.

entries.question: What information is shown in the identity hero section?
entries.answer: The identity hero section shows your avatar, username, email, organization, and join date.

entries.question: How do I reopen a previous scan report?
entries.answer: You can reopen a previous scan report by tapping on the scan row in the Recent Scans list.

entries.question: What shortcuts are available for admins and owners?
entries.answer: Admins and owners have shortcuts to the Administration and Integrations sections, which are role-gated and only visible to them.

entries.question: How do I sign out of my account?
entries.answer: You can sign out of your account by confirming the sign-out prompt. Note that you will need to sign in again to access your account.

entries.question: Why are my scans not showing up in the Recent Scans list?
entries.answer: Scans are fetched for the signed-in user and rendered newest-first. If your scans are not showing up, try checking your account and scan history to ensure that the scans are stored and synced correctly.

entries.question: Can I access my scan history across devices?
entries.answer: Yes, your scan history is account-backed and follows you across devices. You can access your scan history from any device where you are signed in to your account.
symptoms: Scans not available on other devices

entries.question: What types of media can I use to scan a rack?
entries.answer: You can use a photo, video, or AR session from your device camera, or upload an image or video file (JPG, PNG, HEIC/HEIF, MP4, MOV, WEBM).

entries.question: How do I link a service incident to a rack scan?
entries.answer: You can link a service incident to a rack scan by selecting the incident before scanning the rack. This will target the exact device and port and verify the correct rack before scoring.

entries.question: What happens if the quality of my scan is poor?
entries.answer: If the quality of your scan is poor, the quality gate will prevent the scan from being processed. You will be prompted to retake the scan or proceed anyway.

entries.question: Can I scan a tall rack with RackTrack?
entries.answer: Yes, you can scan a tall rack with RackTrack using multi-photo mode. This mode stitches several overlapping shots into one panorama, allowing you to capture a rack taller than a single frame accurately.

entries.question: What is the output of a rack scan?
entries.answer: The output of a rack scan is a completed scan opened on the Results screen, which includes detected devices, port layout, cabling, and a rack group (if the input was a video or multiple racks).

entries.question: How do I access the results of a rack scan?
entries.answer: You can access the results of a rack scan by opening the Results screen. The results will be displayed in an annotated rack view, allowing you to explore the detected devices, ports, and cabling.

entries.question: Can I use RackTrack to document a new rack?
entries.answer: Yes, you can use RackTrack to document a new rack. Simply capture the rack and RackTrack will build the full inventory and offer to register it in the CMDB.

entries.question: How do I use RackTrack to work a ticket?
entries.answer: To use RackTrack to work a ticket, link the incident to the rack scan. This will take you straight to the device and port the ticket is about, with a check that it is the right rack.

entries.question: What is the purpose of the quality gate in RackTrack?
entries.answer: The quality gate in RackTrack protects the pipeline from unusable frames by checking the sharpness, framing, and lighting of the scan. If the quality is poor, the scan will not be processed.

entries.question: What is the Rack Topology feature in RackTrack?
entries.answer: The Rack Topology feature provides a 2D and interactive 3D visualization of a rack's devices and cabling, allowing users to understand the physical layout and wiring of the rack.

entries.question: How do I use the Rack Topology feature?
entries.answer: To use the Rack Topology feature, open the Topology for a rack, toggle between 2D elevation and 3D scene, filter cables by type, turn on Capacity to recolor devices by how full they are, and use Trace to find the cabling path between two devices.

entries.question: What is the difference between real and synthetic data in Rack Topology?
entries.answer: Real data in Rack Topology includes devices, classes, U-positions, sizes, port counts, and connected/free state, which come from the scan. Synthetic data includes cable pairings, cable IDs, types, and lengths, which are inferred and not network-verified.

entries.question: How does the Rack Topology feature handle missing pixel data?
entries.answer: When pixel data is missing, the Rack Topology feature uses a deterministic fallback, which means that a fixed ordering is used to ensure that the same scan always yields the same diagram.

entries.question: Can I override the synthetic data in Rack Topology?
entries.answer: Yes, you can override the synthetic data in Rack Topology by providing a curated override file, which replaces the guessed values with real values.

entries.question: What are some common use cases for the Rack Topology feature?
entries.answer: Common use cases for the Rack Topology feature include planning a move, understanding a rack you didn't build, and tracing a run to speed up a hunt.

entries.question: How do I interpret the cable pairings in Rack Topology?
entries.answer: Cable pairings in Rack Topology are synthetic and inferred, and should be treated as plausible placeholder cabling for planning, not verified physical or network-discovered connections, unless a curated override file is provided.

entries.question: What information is displayed in the Info panel of Rack Topology?
entries.answer: The Info panel in Rack Topology displays device ports tables, cable endpoints, and aggregated-link cable lists.

entries.question: How do I use the Trace feature in Rack Topology?
entries.answer: To use the Trace feature in Rack Topology, turn on Trace and tap two devices to find the cabling path between them.

entries.question: What is the purpose of the Capacity mode in Rack Topology?
entries.answer: The Capacity mode in Rack Topology highlights which switches have room before you relocate a server, allowing you to plan a move more effectively.

entries.question: What happens after a scan finishes in RackTrack?
entries.answer: After a scan finishes, you see your rack photo with every device boxed and labeled. You can pick any device, drill into a specific port, and tell the app when it got something wrong.

entries.question: How do I inspect a device in RackTrack?
entries.answer: To inspect a device, open the device dropdown and choose a device to inspect. Then, pick a port type and number, and press Find Port to open the port-detail dashboard.

entries.question: What information does the port-detail dashboard provide?
entries.answer: The port-detail dashboard provides the status of the port, cable type and color, confidence, and the resolved end device.

entries.question: How do I correct a misread device or port count in RackTrack?
entries.answer: To correct a misread device or port count, answer the confirm/correct prompts for device type and port count. Your corrections will be stored and reused.

entries.question: What is the purpose of the feedback loop in RackTrack?
entries.answer: The feedback loop captures each correction and uses it to retrain the models, so accuracy improves where your fleet differs from the training set.

entries.question: How does RackTrack handle empty or unidentified rack rows?
entries.answer: Empty, closed, and unidentified rack rows are excluded from the overlay and the device picker, so they don't clutter the view.

entries.question: What is the benefit of using RackTrack for verifying an install?
entries.answer: RackTrack allows you to scan, confirm the switch and port count, and trust the rest, documenting the rack in seconds.

entries.question: How does RackTrack help with chasing a bad port?
entries.answer: RackTrack allows you to select a port and see its live status and the device on the other end without opening a terminal.

entries.question: What is the purpose of the 'Your correction' badge in RackTrack?
entries.answer: The 'Your correction' badge marks any value that came from you rather than the model, indicating that you have corrected a misread device or port count.

entries.question: How does RackTrack improve accuracy over time?
entries.answer: RackTrack improves accuracy over time by capturing corrections and using them to retrain the models, so accuracy improves where your fleet differs from the training set.

entries.question: What is the SFP Procurement Advisor and what does it do?
entries.answer: The SFP Procurement Advisor is a reference tool that recommends compatible SFP/optical transceiver modules and plug-and-play DAC/AOC cables to purchase for a given switch, along with prices, product photos, and buy links. It is sized to the number of open SFP ports on the switch.

entries.question: How does the SFP Procurement Advisor work?
entries.answer: The advisor runs automatically from the switch's vendor/model, performs a live product search for compatible transceivers, and if nothing is found, uses a built-in fallback catalog. It then recommends a top pick, alternatives, and plug-and-play cables, and computes totals for the number of open SFP ports.

entries.question: What input does the SFP Procurement Advisor use?
entries.answer: The advisor uses the switch's vendor/model and the number of available SFP ports as input. It also uses live product listings and a built-in fallback catalog.

entries.question: What output does the SFP Procurement Advisor produce?
entries.answer: The advisor produces a top-pick module, alternatives, plug-and-play cables, and totals for the number of open SFP ports. It also includes a datasheet link and a note on the provenance of the recommendation.

entries.question: What do I see on screen when using the SFP Procurement Advisor?
entries.answer: You see a slot summary, a hero 'TOP PICK' card, a list of alternatives, a plug-and-play cables grid, and a footer with a datasheet link and a note on the number of modules and sources.

entries.question: Why does the SFP Procurement Advisor use a fallback catalog?
entries.answer: The advisor uses a fallback catalog when the live product search yields nothing usable. The fallback catalog is a manually verified list of compatible modules, but it can go stale if the manufacturer changes its pages.

entries.question: How do I use the SFP Procurement Advisor to order optics for a new switch?
entries.answer: The advisor lists compatible modules and the total to fill every open cage. You can follow the buy link to order the recommended optics.

entries.question: What if the SFP Procurement Advisor returns an empty result?
entries.answer: If the advisor returns an empty result, you can try searching for the switch's vendor/model manually or checking the fallback catalog.

entries.question: Are the prices shown by the SFP Procurement Advisor always up-to-date?
entries.answer: No, the prices shown by the advisor are indicative and may not always be up-to-date. You should confirm the prices with the vendor before ordering.

entries.question: Can I use the SFP Procurement Advisor to choose a short-run link?
entries.answer: Yes, the advisor offers plug-and-play DAC cables for in-rack or adjacent-rack runs.

entries.question: What is the Specifications Lookup feature in RackTrack?
entries.answer: The Specifications Lookup feature allows you to find the datasheet specifications of a device by typing its vendor and model. It pulls the specifications straight from the manufacturer's product page, so you don't have to hunt for a PDF.

entries.question: How do I use the Specifications Lookup feature?
entries.answer: To use the Specifications Lookup feature, type a vendor and model, and RackTrack will pull the device's datasheet specifications. You can use the type-ahead suggestions to help with the vendor. Then, press the 'Get specifications' button to see the highlights block, full spec table, and product-page link.

entries.question: What kind of information can I find using the Specifications Lookup feature?
entries.answer: The Specifications Lookup feature provides a highlights block with 4-5 of the most decision-relevant specs, a full spec table with every extracted name/value pair, and a product-page link. You can find information such as ports, throughput, layer, power, PoE, uplinks, and more.

entries.question: What if the Specifications Lookup feature can't find the specifications for a device?
entries.answer: If the Specifications Lookup feature can't find the specifications for a device, it will display an 'couldn't extract' message with a link to the product page. It will never provide filler or invented data.

entries.question: Can I use the Specifications Lookup feature to compare devices?
entries.answer: Yes, you can use the Specifications Lookup feature to compare devices. For example, you can pull specs for two switches and compare their PoE budget and MAC table size.

entries.question: Is the data provided by the Specifications Lookup feature real or synthetic?
entries.answer: The data provided by the Specifications Lookup feature is real and live, extracted from the vendor's product page. It is not synthetic or filled with placeholder specs.

entries.question: What are some common use cases for the Specifications Lookup feature?
entries.answer: Some common use cases for the Specifications Lookup feature include sizing an uplink, comparing two switches, and checking throughput and uplink options before committing to a model.

entries.question: What is the Live Switch Data feature in RackTrack?
entries.answer: The Live Switch Data feature in RackTrack provides detailed information about a detected switch, including its identity, specifications, firmware, and optics. It brings together all the relevant data about a switch in one place, driven by what the photo actually saw. It also opens a live session to the switch to report how many ports are free versus in use, and whether an open port is copper or fiber, so you can see at a glance whether there is room to plug something in.
symptoms: How many free ports do I have?
What type of ports are available?
What does the Live Switch Data feature do?

entries.question: How do I access the Live Switch Data feature?
entries.answer: To access the Live Switch Data feature, pick a switch from the detected list, and then confirm its identity. You can then view its specifications, firmware, and SFP advisor tabs. You can also reach the live port list from the Ports view for a rack, where the server opens a session to the switch and requests its interface status; the filter pills then narrow the list.
symptoms: How do I get a list of available ports?
How do I use the Live Switch Data feature?

entries.question: What if the switch's identity was not read correctly?
entries.answer: If the switch's identity was not read correctly, you can type or correct it in the inline editor. This will allow you to access the correct information for the switch.

entries.question: How does the Live Switch Data feature get its information?
entries.answer: The Live Switch Data feature gets its information from a combination of sources, including the scanned identity of the switch, live vendor and firmware lookups, and a curated map of official vendor portal and download pages.

entries.question: What kind of information can I find in the Specifications tab?
entries.answer: The Specifications tab provides a live datasheet lookup for the switch, including its specifications and a product-page link.

entries.question: How does the Firmware tab work?
entries.answer: The Firmware tab provides the latest version of the firmware for the switch, as well as upgrade guidance. It compares the entered current version against the latest version found in the vendor's release notes.

entries.question: What is the SFP Advisor tab used for?
entries.answer: The SFP Advisor tab provides recommendations for compatible transceivers and cables for the switch.

entries.question: Can I manually enter the make and model of a switch?
entries.answer: Yes, you can manually enter the make and model of a switch if it was not detected correctly. This information will be saved locally and will survive re-scans.

entries.question: How does the Live Switch Data feature handle multiple switches?
entries.answer: The Live Switch Data feature allows you to pick a switch from the detected list and view its information. If several switches were detected, you can switch between them using the tab strip.

entries.question: What are some common use cases for the Live Switch Data feature?
entries.answer: Some common use cases for the Live Switch Data feature include auditing a switch on sight, fixing a bad read, and planning optics for a switch.

entries.question: What is RackTrack, and what does it do?
entries.short: RackTrack turns a photo of a datacenter rack into a documented inventory. You photograph the rack, it identifies the devices and their ports, and you confirm or correct what it found.
entries.answer:
RackTrack turns a photo of a datacenter rack into a documented inventory, so a rack can be recorded in seconds instead of by hand.

The basic flow: photograph the rack, and the app comes back with your photo with every device boxed and labelled. You can pick any device, drill into a specific port, and tell the app when it got something wrong.

From there it also:
1. Reads the switch live over the network, so you can see which ports are in use, available or reserved right now.
2. Draws the rack as a 2D and interactive 3D layout, so you can see the physical wiring.
3. Registers the devices, ports and connections into your CMDB, and flags anything that disagrees with your existing records.
4. Looks up manufacturer datasheet specifications from a vendor and model.
5. Records every port change over time, so re-cabling and flapping links show up.
6. Scans several racks at once from a video pan or a set of photos, and groups them into a row.
symptoms: what is the workflow of racktrack
how does racktrack work end to end

entries.question: What are ports, and what does the Ports screen show?
entries.short: Ports are the sockets on a switch that cables plug into. The Ports screen signs in to the switch over the network and reads them live, showing which are in use, available or reserved.
entries.answer:
Ports are the sockets on a switch that cables plug into — RJ45, SFP, Console and USB are the types RackTrack recognises.

Open the rack, then open Ports. This screen signs in to the switch over the network and reads it live — it is not built from your photo. At the top you get three tiles: In use (ports with a live link, out of the total), Available (ports you can plug into today) and Identified (ports where the far-end device announced itself over LLDP/CDP). Below that are three tabs: Ports, Cables and Ping.

How a port is classified:
1. Available — the port is link down and has no description. This is spare capacity you can use today.
2. In use — the port is link up or connected.
3. Reserved — the port is administratively down, shut or err-disabled, or it is down but still has a description. Reserved ports do not count as open capacity.

Copper or fiber is taken from the switch's medium column, or inferred from the interface naming or the SFP-cage count from your scan.
symptoms: what does the ports screen show
how does it know which ports are free

entries.question: What is a rack scan, and how does it work?
entries.short: A scan is a photo of a rack that RackTrack analyses to find the devices and their ports. When it finishes you get your photo with every device boxed and labelled, and you can correct anything it misread.
entries.answer:
A scan is a photo of a rack that RackTrack analyses to identify what is installed.

When a scan finishes you see your rack photo with every device boxed and labelled. You can pick any device, drill into a specific port, and tell the app when it got something wrong — those corrections are how it improves.

You can scan more than one rack at a time: pan a video across several racks, or upload photos of each one. RackTrack splits the video or photos into individual racks, analyses each, and groups them so you can view the whole row in 3D.

The point of scanning rather than typing is speed with a check at the end: scan, confirm the switch and port count, and trust the rest.
symptoms: how do I scan a rack

entries.question: What is a rack, and what does the Topology view show?
entries.short: A rack is the cabinet of stacked equipment you are documenting. The Topology view draws it as a 2D and interactive 3D picture of the devices and their cabling.
entries.answer:
A rack is the cabinet of stacked network and server equipment you are documenting — RackTrack works one rack at a time unless you use a multi-rack scan.

The Rack Topology view provides a 2D and interactive 3D visualisation of a rack's devices and cabling, so you can understand the physical layout and how it is wired without standing in front of it.

If you scanned several racks together, they are grouped so you can view the entire row in 3D.
symptoms: what does the topology view show

entries.question: Do I need to be logged in to scan a rack?
entries.answer: Yes. Scanning is no longer anonymous — the upload requires a valid login, and so does saving any correction afterwards. If you are signed out, the app sends you to the login screen and returns you to where you were once you are in.

entries.question: I signed my company up and I cannot scan or add anyone. Why?
entries.answer: A self-signup creates an organization in a pending state. It cannot add members or run scans until the platform owner approves it. You will wait on an approval screen that advances automatically the moment approval lands. (Organizations that the platform owner creates directly are active straight away.)

entries.question: Why does it only let me sign up with a Gmail address?
entries.answer: Public self-signup is deliberately limited to @gmail.com addresses. Existing staff and owner accounts, invites and password resets are not subject to that rule — it applies only to the public signup path.

entries.question: What kinds of equipment can RackTrack recognise?
entries.answer: The device model recognises twelve classes: Closed Unit, Empty, Firewall, Gateway, Load Balancer, PDU, Patch Panel, Router, Server, Storage unit, Switch and UPS. "Closed Unit" and "Empty" are slot placeholders rather than equipment.

entries.question: What does it mean when a port says "unknown"?
entries.answer: It means RackTrack could not measure whether that port has a cable. Occupancy comes only from the status sweep; when the sweep cannot tag a port, RackTrack reports "unknown" rather than guessing. It specifically does not use the cable-colour classifier to decide occupancy, because that model only identifies a colour and has no way to say whether a cable is present at all.

entries.question: If two people scan the exact same photo, do they see each other's data?
entries.answer: No. The same image produces the same RK-… id and shares one folder on disk, but ownership is recorded per site, and the access rule (owner → all; org admin → their org's racks; everyone else → their own site's racks, failing closed) is what governs who can open it. Neither tenant can see the other's ownership or view of it.

entries.question: Who can use Ground Truth?
entries.answer: Ground Truth is owner-only for now, enforced on the server. It is per-scan — you reach it from a specific rack's results after analysis — and it lists only the real devices in that scan, dropping the "Empty" and "Closed Unit" slot rows while keeping "Unidentified" rows (those are what most need labelling).

entries.question: Can I scan two racks at once?
entries.answer: Yes — use "Scan two racks". Pick two images, or a single video that pans across both; RackTrack picks the best frame of each rack, detects both, and produces a combined view including the cabling that crosses between them, with a 3D combined topology. Each rack still exists on its own with all its normal views, and a rack-tabs strip lets you move between the members of the group.

entries.question: Does RackTrack connect to my live switches?
entries.answer: Only when you ask it to. Live-switch access is opt-in: for switches you choose to monitor, it connects over SSH on a schedule to read real port state and record drift over time. It never reaches into your equipment in the background.

entries.question: What is the difference between the Network tab and the Switches tab?
entries.answer: The Network tab matches the physical devices in a scan to what the live network can actually see (LLDP neighbours and learned MACs) through the discovery back-end. The Switches tab is driven by your records database (CMDB) and lists the switches associated with the rack, with details such as firmware.

entries.question: Is there a dark mode?
entries.answer: No. RackTrack uses a single light theme by design — flat white surfaces and one consistent look across every screen.

entries.question: What is "Ask DOT" and can it make things up?
entries.short: Ask DOT is the built-in support assistant.
entries.answer: Ask DOT is the built-in support assistant. It answers only from RackTrack's own verified knowledge base. When search is confident it returns the verified answer word-for-word (nothing is generated, so nothing can be invented). When a question is relevant but needs phrasing, it can use a language model to compose a grounded answer — preferring a hosted model (OpenRouter, defaulting to NVIDIA's Nemotron on the free tier) when configured, falling back to a local model (Ollama), and, with neither available, degrading to the verbatim knowledge-base answers. When nothing relevant matches, it refuses and points you to a human rather than guessing.

entries.question: How do I reach a real person?
entries.answer: Use the Contact screen (also where Ask DOT's "reach a person" hand-off leads). It emails the RackTrack support team; support can reply to you directly.

entries.question: What happens if one of the connected systems is down?
entries.answer: The product keeps working. Every external integration — the records database, live discovery, the payment provider for the marketplace, the support bot's language-model back-ends — is optional and fail-soft: if it is missing or unreachable, that one feature turns off or returns a clear "not available", and the rest of RackTrack is unaffected.

entries.question: Which should I use — the app or the browser?
entries.short: Both come from the same product and have the same features. The mobile app (iPhone, iPad, Android) is best for a technician standing in front of a rack with a camera; the browser version on a laptop or desktop is better for reviewing results, running reports and administration. The layout adapts to the screen — a sidebar on wide screens, a bottom bar on a phone — but the words and features are identical.
entries.answer:
Both come from the same product and have the same features. The mobile app (iPhone, iPad, Android) is best for a technician standing in front of a rack with a camera; the browser version on a laptop or desktop is better for reviewing results, running reports and administration. The layout adapts to the screen — a sidebar on wide screens, a bottom bar on a phone — but the words and features are identical.

entries.question: How do I sign out?
entries.answer: On a phone: open Profile (bottom-right tab), tap the sign-out icon at the top-right, then confirm Sign out. On desktop/iPad: click Sign out at the bottom of the left sidebar.

entries.question: Where is the sign-out button?
entries.answer: On a phone it's on the Profile page, top-right corner. On desktop or iPad it's at the bottom of the left sidebar. The waiting-for-approval screen and the desktop welcome screen also have their own Sign out buttons.

entries.question: How do I sign up?
entries.answer: Go to Create an organization from the sign-in page (/signup). Enter a @gmail.com email, a username (3–32 chars), your organization name, and a strong password. Then verify the 6-digit code sent to your email. Note your new organization then waits for the platform owner to approve it.

entries.question: Do I need a Gmail to sign up?
entries.answer: For creating your own organization, yes — self sign-up only accepts @gmail.com addresses. If you're invited to an existing team, no — the invite can be for any email address.

entries.question: What are the password rules?
entries.answer: At least 8 characters, and it must include an uppercase letter, a lowercase letter, a digit, and a special character. The sign-up screen shows a live strength bar telling you what's still missing.

entries.question: What are the username rules?
entries.answer: 3 to 32 characters, using only letters, digits, and the symbols . _ -.

entries.question: I forgot my password.
entries.answer: Tap Forgot password? on the sign-in screen. Enter your email, get the 6-digit code by email, type it in, then either set a new password or choose "No, take me to the app" to get in without changing it.

entries.question: How do I reset my password?
entries.answer: Sign-in page → Forgot password? → enter email → enter the 6-digit code from your email → Yes, change password → set a new strong password. You're signed in right after.

entries.question: How do I change my password?
entries.answer: Use the Forgot password? flow on the sign-in page — that's how you set a new password (enter email, enter the emailed code, then choose "Yes, change password"). There is no separate "change password" screen inside the app.

entries.question: Why was I signed out?
entries.answer: Usually one of: your 30-day sign-in expired, you (or the app) cleared saved data, you're in a private/incognito window, or an admin deactivated/removed your account. Just sign in again — no data is lost.

entries.question: How long does a sign-in last?
entries.answer: 30 days on that device. After that you sign in again.

entries.question: How long do I stay logged in?
entries.answer: About a month — 30 days per device — unless you sign out or your saved data is cleared.

entries.question: Do I have to log in every time I open the app?
entries.answer: No. You stay signed in for 30 days, so you can close and reopen the app freely without logging in again.

entries.question: How do I use an invite code?
entries.answer: Open the invite link your admin sent you (it looks like /invite/…). It shows the team you're joining; choose a username and password, tap Join, and you're in. No email code needed. Invite links expire after 7 days and work once.

entries.question: Someone sent me an invite — what do I do?
entries.answer: Tap the link, pick a username and a strong password on the page that opens, and tap Join. You'll be signed into their organization immediately.

entries.question: My invite link doesn't work / says expired.
entries.answer: Invite links last 7 days and can only be used once. If yours has expired or was already used, ask your admin to send a new one.

entries.question: What does "pending approval" mean?
entries.answer: You created a new organization and it hasn't been approved by the RackTrack platform owner yet. You wait on a screen that checks automatically and lets you in the moment they approve it. This only happens for self-created organizations.

entries.question: How long does approval take?
entries.answer: The screen says it "usually doesn't take long" and it checks every few seconds automatically. The exact timing is up to the platform owner — you're let in as soon as they approve.

entries.question: Do I need an account?
entries.answer: Yes. RackTrack is behind a login — you can't scan or use any real feature without signing in.

entries.question: Can I use it without logging in?
entries.answer: No. Logged out, you only see the welcome screen; every real action sends you to sign in. You need an account (created by you, or via an invite) to actually use it.

entries.question: Can I sign in with my email instead of my username?
entries.answer: Yes. On the sign-in screen the "Username or email" field accepts either — type whichever you remember.

entries.question: What do I put in the Organization box when signing in?
entries.answer: Usually nothing — leave it blank. It's optional and only needed in the rare case where the same username exists in more than one organization.

entries.question: Can I join a company that already uses RackTrack?
entries.answer: Only if they invite you. There's no public "join" button — ask that company's admin for an invite link or for a username and password.

entries.question: Why won't it let me create an account with my work email?
entries.answer: Self sign-up only accepts @gmail.com addresses. To use a work email, get invited to a team on that address instead.

entries.question: I never got my verification / reset code.
entries.answer: Codes are emailed and expire in about a minute, so check straight away (and your spam folder). If it didn't arrive or expired, tap Resend for a fresh code and enter it quickly.

entries.question: Does signing out on my phone sign me out on my laptop?
entries.answer: No. Sign-ins are per device. Signing out on one device leaves your other devices signed in until they expire or you sign out on each.

entries.question: Will I lose my scans if I sign out or get signed out?
entries.answer: No. Your scans and organization live on the server, not on your device. Signing back in brings everything back.

entries.question: Can I stay signed in on more than one device?
entries.answer: Yes. Each device keeps its own 30-day sign-in, so you can be signed in on your phone, tablet, and computer at the same time.

entries.question: How do I get back in after being signed out?
entries.answer: Just go to the sign-in screen and enter your username (or email) and password. If you've forgotten the password, use Forgot password?.

entries.question: Is DOT going to make something up?
entries.answer: No. Everything it tells you comes from a verified knowledge-base entry — copied word for word, or rephrased by a model that's only allowed to use the matched entries and is checked before you see it. If it can't ground an answer, it refuses.

entries.question: What does the "Verified answer" badge mean?
entries.answer: That the reply is a verbatim, human-checked answer straight from the knowledge base — nothing was generated. "Composed from documentation" means a model tidied up matched entries; "No verified answer" means DOT declined.

entries.question: DOT said it doesn't know. Now what?
entries.answer: Tap "Contact support" under the reply. It opens the Contact page pre-filled with your question and emails the RackTrack support team at support@racktrack.ai, with your details attached and Reply-To set to you.

entries.question: I pasted my password by accident — what happens?
entries.answer: DOT stops and shows a "Security notice" instead of answering. It asks you to change the password now (it may be stored in the chat) and then re-describe the problem without it. It never needs your password to help.

entries.question: Does DOT work if the AI model is down?
entries.answer: Yes. It falls back to giving verified answers and honest refusals without the model. You'll still get every documented answer; you just won't get the "composed" phrasing for fuzzy questions.

entries.question: Why did DOT give me a numbered list instead of an answer?
entries.answer: It found a few possible matches but wasn't sure which you meant. Tap the one that fits and it'll answer that from the verified text — better than guessing wrong.

entries.question: Can I ask about pricing, the roadmap, or how RackTrack compares to another tool?
entries.answer: DOT will politely decline those — it only knows how the app works today, not commercial or future plans, and it won't compare RackTrack to other products. It'll point you to your administrator or account manager.

entries.question: Will a member see admin-only answers?
entries.answer: Everyone currently gets the same single knowledge base, which includes admin how-to entries. What's fully walled off is a set of internal-only entries (server file paths and line numbers) that exist to maintain the KB and are never used to answer anyone.

entries.question: How many questions can I ask?
entries.answer: Up to 60 an hour, with room for a quick burst of 10. That comfortably covers a whole troubleshooting session; if you somehow hit it, DOT tells you exactly how long to wait.

entries.question: Is my question stored anywhere?
entries.answer: Only when DOT couldn't answer it. Refused questions are logged (question text plus the near-miss entries and your user id) so the team can grow the knowledge base to cover the gap. Answered questions aren't stored as a transcript.

entries.question: Where does the "Contact support" email actually go?
entries.answer: To support@racktrack.ai — via the support Microsoft 365 mailbox where configured, otherwise over SMTP — with Reply-To set to your email so the reply comes straight back to you.

entries.question: Is DOT the same in the floating panel and the Help page?
entries.answer: Yes — same assistant, same knowledge base, same rules. The floating Assist panel is for a quick answer mid-task; the full-screen DOT / Help page is for when you came to ask something and want the starters, badges, and tap-able options.

entries.question: Where do I add a connection?
entries.answer: Open your Profile and tap the Data Sources card (it says "Connect a database" if nothing is set up yet), then press Add connection. Only owners and organization admins can reach this screen.

entries.question: Can I have more than one connection at once?
entries.answer: You can save as many as you like, but only one is active at a time. The active one is what the whole app reads from. Press Use on any saved connection to switch; the app re-reads its data from the new source. There is no blending of two sources at once.

entries.question: Why can't I see my saved password?
entries.answer: Because credentials are write-only on purpose. They're encrypted and never sent back to any screen — not even masked with dots. This is a security promise: a secret can go in, but it can never come back out.

entries.question: How do I change a password or token?
entries.answer: Open the connection's ⋯ menu, choose Edit, and type the new value into just the field you want to replace. Leave the other credential fields blank to keep what's already saved, then press Save changes.

entries.question: Why can't I change a connection's type after creating it?
entries.answer: Each system needs a different set of fields, so the Type is locked once the connection exists. If you need a different kind of system, add a new connection.

entries.question: What does "Refresh data from this source" do, and why only for ServiceNow?
entries.answer: It pulls the latest incidents from your active ServiceNow instance in the background and updates the banner with the result. Only ServiceNow shows this button because the live refresh (and the registration and reconciliation flows) are built around ServiceNow today.

entries.question: Reconciliation says a device is a "mismatch" — what does that mean?
entries.answer: It means what your records expect at that rack slot and what the camera actually saw disagree — either nothing was detected there, or a different type of device was. That's physical drift. Go verify at the rack, and either move the device to where the CMDB says, or update the CMDB if it really did move.

entries.question: It says "low confidence" instead of a clean match — do I have drift?
entries.answer: Not necessarily. The right kind of device was seen at the right slot, but the photo wasn't clear enough to be sure. Rescan with better lighting or a straighter angle before sending anyone to the rack.

entries.question: How does RackTrack match a scan to my CMDB when the scan doesn't know device names?
entries.answer: It matches by position and type, not by name. It takes each CMDB record, works out the U position and the visual class it should be, and checks whether the scan detected that class at that U. Names are the CMDB's job; the camera only knows "a Switch at U10", so that's what the comparison uses.

entries.question: Does registering a rack write to my CMDB immediately?
entries.answer: No. Registration always opens a Service Request first and only writes once that request is approved in ServiceNow. Every CMDB write is gated behind an approval — that's the core compliance promise. (There's a demo-only shortcut for owners, but it's disabled unless someone explicitly turns it on.)

entries.question: Will re-scanning the same rack create duplicate records or duplicate tickets?
entries.answer: No. Writes are idempotent and rack-scoped — re-running against an unchanged scan changes nothing. And RackTrack fingerprints the difference between scan and records: an unchanged difference raises nothing, and a changed one appends a note instead of opening a second request.

entries.question: The refresh failed and mentions the instance being asleep — what now?
entries.short: ServiceNow developer instances go to sleep. Open your instance in a browser (<instance>.service-now.com), sign in to confirm it's awake, then press Refresh data from this source again. The failure banner tells you exactly this.
entries.answer:
ServiceNow developer instances go to sleep. Open your instance in a browser (<instance>.service-now.com), sign in to confirm it's awake, then press Refresh data from this source again. The failure banner tells you exactly this.
