entries.question: Does one photo really produce the whole inventory?
entries.answer: Yes. A single front-of-rack photo drives device detection, the U grid, and port classification. Video is reduced to a best frame first; a multi-rack pan is split into one frame per rack, each analysed independently.

entries.question: Why did my rack come back with a row labelled "Unidentified"?
entries.answer: Either no detector produced a confident class for that row (so a synthetic placeholder fills it), or a port-bearing device was demoted because no ports were found on it. It's kept visible so the row isn't lost, but it's hidden from the port picker.

entries.question: The pipeline said a switch has 24 ports but I only see cables on some — how does it know which are used?
entries.answer: Port count comes from the type model (ports_9.pt); occupancy comes from a separate status model (port_count.pt). A port with no status match reads unknown, not "empty" — the pipeline won't guess.

entries.question: It found no ports on my server / storage array. Bug?
entries.answer: No. Port detection runs only on Switch, Patch Panel, Firewall, Gateway, and Router. Servers, storage, and blank panels are intentionally skipped to avoid hallucinated ports. PDUs get power-outlet detection instead.

entries.question: Why does my 26-port switch report as 24?
entries.answer: Patch panels snap to 24/48, but switches don't — a switch count comes from the visual detector (optionally corrected by faceplate OCR). If a count looks off, cable occlusion or a two-row layout is the usual cause; the relabel flow lets an operator set the true count, which is stored as port_count_source: "user_relabeled".

entries.question: How does it decide the U numbers?
entries.answer: It measures one rack unit from the median height of detected switches (or patch panels), tiles a gap-free grid anchored to real equipment, and numbers from the bottom up (u01 at the bottom), the standard rack convention.

entries.question: Can the cable colour be wrong?
entries.answer: The cable model names connector + colour on ports already known to be connected. It has no "no-cable" class, so it's never used to decide whether a cable is present — only what it is. Operator colour corrections are learned and reapplied on later scans of the same rack.

entries.question: My rack is buried in cables. Will the scan still work?
entries.answer: It may warn or hard-stop for occlusion and suggest side-angle photos. You can proceed anyway, but devices hidden behind bundles can be missed — that's exactly what the warning is about.

entries.question: Where's the data the app shows me?
entries.answer: Everything comes from outputs/<rackId>/device_unit_map.json, read by buildResponse(). The images you see are 2_devices_only.png (device boxes) and 7_rack_all_ports.png (the port overlay).

entries.question: What if the model files aren't deployed?
entries.answer: The occlusion gate falls back to a heuristic rather than blocking uploads; the OCR grounding becomes a no-op; missing port models simply yield zero ports (and demotion). The pipeline is built to degrade rather than hard-fail closed.

entries.question: Does "seg" vs "dual" change my results?
entries.answer: The live config runs seg (single devices_seg.pt). dual (two models, Server-only + general) is fully coded but not selected by the current models map. Both return the same shape, so nothing downstream changes if the mode is flipped.

entries.question: Is the port numbering stable if I re-scan?
entries.answer: Numbering is spatial (column-major, bottom-anchored units), so it's reproducible for the same layout. A user-confirmed count forces exactly that many main ports so "port 24" stays the 24th physical position on later selects.

entries.question: What does each model actually do?
entries.answer: devices_seg.pt finds the equipment (12 classes). ports_9.pt names each port's type (9 classes). port_count.pt says whether each port is connected or empty and gives the count (2 classes). pdu_ports_v1_det_best.pt does the same for PDU power outlets (2 classes). cable_eff_best names a cable's connector + colour (14 classes). rack_classifier.pth decides if the whole photo is clear or too occluded to trust (2 classes).

entries.question: Why are there so many models instead of one?
entries.answer: Because each narrow model is more accurate, easier to retrain, and fails independently. A device model asked to also learn ports, cables, and photo quality would be worse at all of them, and a single unsure answer would taint the whole report.

entries.question: Why are ports sometimes 0?
entries.answer: Most often the port models weren't available (files missing / wrong path), so the port stage detected nothing and the device came back with port_count = 0. It can also happen on genuinely portless or fully cable-occluded faces, or when the status model (port_count.pt, the weakest-trained one) under-detects on a dark/blurry crop — in which case ports may show but their status reads unknown.

entries.question: Which model detects the devices, and what can it recognise?
entries.answer: devices_seg.pt, a YOLOv8m-seg model with exactly 12 classes: Closed Unit, Empty, Firewall, Gateway, Load Balancer, PDU, Patch Panel, Router, Server, Storage unit, Switch, UPS.

entries.question: Why are there *two* port models for the same ports?
entries.answer: They answer different questions. ports_9.pt gives the type (RJ45 / SFP / console / USB …) but no status; port_count.pt gives the status (connected / empty) but no type. The pipeline runs both and matches their boxes so each port ends up with both a type and a status.

entries.question: Why does a PDU need its own model?
entries.answer: Power outlets look nothing like network ports, so pdu_ports_v1_det_best.pt is trained only on power_port_connected / power_port_empty. It counts outlets and reports whether the rack is powered.

entries.question: How does the cable classifier know the colour and connector?
entries.answer: cable_eff_best (EfficientNet-B0) classifies a cable crop into one of 14 labels combining connector and colour (e.g. RJ_45 Blue, LC_Aqua, SC_Orange). Code then splits that into (connector, colour). It knows three connector families: RJ-45, LC, SC.

entries.question: Where do the class names come from — are they hard-coded?
entries.answer: The four YOLO models carry their own class names inside the model file, so they're self-describing and were read straight from those files for this doc. The cable classifier is the exception: its file holds only the weights, so its 14 labels are stored separately and must match the training folder order.
entries.short: The YOLO models store their own class names; only the cable classifier keeps its 14 labels separately, matching training folder order.

entries.question: What is the occlusion model and when does it run?
entries.answer: rack_classifier.pth (MobileNetV2, classes clear / occluded) runs on upload, before analysis. If it's ≥ 0.55 sure the rack is occluded it hard-stops and asks for side-angle photos; 0.50–0.55 is a soft warning; below that it's clear. If the model or torch is missing, it falls back to a heuristic and never blocks the upload.

entries.question: Do these run on real photos or a simulation?
entries.answer: Real photos, always. There is no fake-data mode. "Synthetic" in the code refers only to filling grid gaps and drawing port cells to keep the layout complete — the actual classifications always come from a model looking at the real image, and unclaimed rows are labelled "Unidentified," never a false "Empty."

entries.question: What architecture and training settings do the models use?
entries.short: The four detectors are all YOLOv8m (medium) — segmentation for devices, detection for the three port/PDU models — trained at image size 640. devices_seg.pt, ports_9.pt, and pdu_ports_v1_det_best.pt used AdamW at LR 0.001 for 100/100/120 epochs; port_count.pt used the "auto" optimizer at LR 0.01 (saved at epoch 19).
entries.answer: The four detectors are all YOLOv8m (medium) — segmentation for devices, detection for the three port/PDU models — trained at image size 640. devices_seg.pt, ports_9.pt, and pdu_ports_v1_det_best.pt used AdamW at LR 0.001 for 100/100/120 epochs; port_count.pt used the "auto" optimizer at LR 0.01 (saved at epoch 19). The two classifiers are torchvision models: EfficientNet-B0 for cables (256×256, no normalization) and MobileNetV2 for occlusion (224×224, ImageNet normalization).

entries.question: A model file is missing on a machine — what breaks?
entries.answer: Only that model's stage. Missing device model → no devices. Missing port models → port_count = 0, ports empty. Missing PDU model → PDUs show 0 outlets. Missing cable model → cables unlabelled. Missing occlusion model → falls back to the heuristic gate. The Models/ folder is git-ignored, so weights must be staged onto each machine separately from the code.

entries.question: What are the 12 classes?
entries.answer: The same 12: Closed Unit, Empty, Firewall, Gateway, Load Balancer, PDU, Patch Panel, Router, Server, Storage unit, Switch, UPS. "Base classes" means the types the shape AI can output before any text is read.

entries.question: Which devices does RackTrack identify?
entries.answer: From shape alone it identifies these 12: Closed Unit, Empty, Firewall, Gateway, Load Balancer, PDU, Patch Panel, Router, Server, Storage unit, Switch, UPS. After reading the text it can also mark a device as Controller, Recorder, Amplifier, or Modem.

entries.question: What devices can it detect?
entries.answer: The 12 shape classes above. Reading the front-panel text can additionally upgrade a device to Controller, Recorder, Amplifier, or Modem.

entries.question: What device types does it recognise?
entries.answer: Twelve by shape (Closed Unit, Empty, Firewall, Gateway, Load Balancer, PDU, Patch Panel, Router, Server, Storage unit, Switch, UPS) plus four more that only come from reading text (Controller, Recorder, Amplifier, Modem).

entries.question: Does it detect servers?
entries.answer: Yes. Server is one of the 12 classes, and there is a dedicated detection pass focused on finding servers.

entries.question: Can it detect switches?
entries.answer: Yes. Switch is one of the 12 classes and is usually the most common device found in a rack.

entries.question: Can it identify a firewall?
entries.answer: Yes. Firewall is one of the 12 shape classes. On top of that, brands like Palo Alto, FortiGate/Fortinet, and Check Point in the front-panel text will confirm a device as a Firewall.

entries.question: What is a Closed Unit?
entries.answer: A blanking or filler panel, or any sealed-front unit that has no visible ports. It occupies a rack slot but is not a working networked device, so RackTrack hides it from the results view.

entries.question: What is an Empty unit / Empty slot?
entries.answer: A rack slot with nothing installed in it — just the open rails. It is one of the 12 classes but is hidden on the results screen because there is nothing to inspect.

entries.question: What is the difference between Empty and Unidentified?
entries.answer: "Empty" means the model is confident the slot is bare. "Unidentified" is a placeholder for a slot that clearly holds something but that nothing managed to classify — RackTrack refuses to call it Empty because that would be a false certainty. Both are hidden from the annotated view.

entries.question: Why do I see "Controller" or "Recorder" when those aren't in the 12 classes?
entries.answer: Because RackTrack read the text on the device. The shape model guessed one of the 12, then OCR found a brand (for example Planar → Controller, Sony → Recorder) or a label code and upgraded the device to that more accurate type. These four extra types — Controller, Recorder, Amplifier, Modem — only ever come from reading text.

entries.question: Why does the same device show as a different type on a second scan?
entries.answer: The first scan may have used the shape guess only, and the second scan managed to read the brand or label text and upgraded the type. Clearer photos give the text step more to work with.

entries.question: What is a Load Balancer?
entries.answer: A device that spreads network traffic across several servers so no single server is overloaded. It is one of the 12 shape classes (position 4 in the model) and can also be set from a LB code in a device's label.

entries.question: Is Load Balancer detected by shape or only by text?
entries.answer: By shape — it is one of the 12 base classes — and it can additionally be confirmed by an LB label code. It is not one of the text-only types.

entries.question: Does RackTrack detect PSU (power supply unit)?
entries.answer: Not automatically. There is no PSU class in the shape model, so it is never a raw detection. PSU is available as a manual correction label, and it can be applied when an OCR'd label contains a PSU code.

entries.question: What is a PDU?
entries.answer: A Power Distribution Unit — the rack's power strip that feeds mains power to the other devices, usually with a row of outlets. It is one of the 12 classes and has its own power-outlet view when selected.

entries.question: What is the difference between a PDU and a UPS?
entries.answer: A PDU just distributes mains power to outlets. A UPS is a battery backup that keeps equipment running through a power cut. Both are separate classes among the 12.

entries.question: What is a Storage unit?
entries.answer: A disk array or NAS whose main job is to store data. It is one of the 12 classes. Note it is not offered in the correction picker, so you cannot hand-relabel a device to "Storage unit".

entries.question: What's the difference between the model classes and the correction options?
entries.answer: The 12 model classes are what the shape AI can output. The 14 correction options are what you can label a device as when you fix a mistake. Nine types are in both. The model also has Closed Unit, Empty, and Storage unit (not in the correction list); the correction list also has Modem, Controller, Recorder, Amplifier, and PSU (which the model never auto-detects).

entries.question: Why can I pick PSU or Modem as a correction if RackTrack can't detect them?
entries.answer: The correction list is about what a human might sensibly call a device, not what the AI can guess. Those human labels are still useful — they feed back into training and produce a correct inventory even for gear the shape model has no class for.

entries.question: How many device types can I choose from when correcting a device?
entries.answer: Fourteen: Switch, Patch Panel, Firewall, Router, Server, Load Balancer, Modem, Controller, Recorder, Amplifier, Gateway, PDU, PSU, UPS. The same list appears on both the Results page and the Ground Truth page.

entries.question: Why isn't "Empty" or "Closed Unit" in the correction list?
entries.answer: Because those are not things you would relabel a real device to. The correction list is for naming actual equipment, so the empty/blank/placeholder types are left out.

entries.question: What does a device name like U18-SW01 mean?
entries.answer: U18 is the rack position (unit 18), SW is the class code for Switch, and 01 means it is the first switch found. RackTrack builds names from position + class code + a running number.

entries.question: What does a name like RVEW-CORE-SW01 mean?
entries.answer: RackTrack read a real label on the rack (RVEW-CORE-SW01), recognised the naming pattern, and reused it to name the other devices in that rack — so their names match your existing scheme instead of the plain U-position names.

entries.question: What are the U codes (u01, u02...)?
entries.answer: They are the rack-unit slots. RackTrack lays a grid of 1U slots down the rack; a device that is two or three units tall claims that many slots. In the main grid, u01 is the bottom slot and the numbers increase upward, following the standard rack convention.

entries.question: Why are some devices missing from the labelled picture?
entries.answer: Empty slots, Closed Units, and Unidentified placeholders are deliberately hidden from the annotated view and the device picker, because there is nothing useful to inspect on them. They may still be counted internally.

entries.question: Which brands upgrade a device's type automatically?
entries.answer: Among others: Planar → Controller; Sony → Recorder; Tripp-Lite → PDU; APC, Eaton, Schneider → UPS; Palo Alto, FortiGate/Fortinet, Check Point → Firewall; Audiocodes, MediaPack, Polycom → Gateway; Cisco, Catalyst, Nexus, Aruba, Juniper, Meraki → Switch; CEdge → Router. RackTrack also allows for common OCR misspellings of these brand names.

entries.question: Does the type on screen change what training data RackTrack keeps?
entries.answer: When you confirm or correct a device, RackTrack writes a feedback record and updates its accuracy scoreboard. Corrections you make on Results and truths you give on Ground Truth are stored the same way, so both improve future detections.

entries.question: How do I fix a wrong device?
entries.answer: On the Results screen, select the device. Under it you'll see "Detected as \<type\> — right?". Tap No, choose the real type from the list (or type it in Other), and submit. RackTrack updates the label everywhere and records the correction. Nothing on the physical device changes.

entries.question: How do I correct the device type specifically?
entries.answer: Same card — "Detected as X — right?" → No → pick the correct type from Switch, Patch Panel, Firewall, Router, Server, Load Balancer, Modem, Controller, Recorder, Amplifier, Gateway, PDU, PSU, UPS, or type your own in Other. Your choice is saved, and the card then reads "Device: <type> — you set this."
entries.short: On the detection card tap No, pick the right device type (or type your own in Other), and it's saved as 'you set this.'

entries.question: How do I tell it a device is a Switch, not a UPS?
entries.answer: Select that device, tap No on "Detected as UPS — right?", choose Switch, and submit. The stored class flips from UPS to Switch, the picker and reports follow immediately, and RackTrack remembers so a similar-looking device auto-reads as a Switch on your next scan.

entries.question: The port count is wrong — how do I fix it?
entries.answer: Answer the device-type question first, then you'll see "Detected N RJ45 ports — right?". Tap No, pick a common count (8/12/16/24/48) or type the exact number, and submit. RackTrack re-lays-out the ports to your number and redraws the device so every port shows.

entries.question: What actually happens when I correct the port count?
entries.answer: The server re-runs port detection for just that device using your number as the target. If it now finds too many, it trims to your count; if too few, it lays out a clean grid of exactly your count (one or two rows, numbered the way the app numbers a switch), copying each real port's connected/empty status. It saves the new layout and redraws the device image.

entries.question: Does correcting the port count change the ports on my actual switch?
entries.answer: No. It only rearranges RackTrack's drawing and record of the ports. The physical ports are untouched — nothing is renumbered, enabled, or disabled on the hardware.

entries.question: Does correcting anything change my switch or other hardware?
entries.answer: No. Every correction edits only RackTrack's stored records and its training data. RackTrack never logs into or alters any device, port, cable, or power. Think of it as fixing notes, not operating equipment.

entries.question: What happens when I say something is wrong?
entries.answer: RackTrack (1) updates its record for this scan, (2) logs the correction to an append-only feedback log, (3) saves a cropped image of the item under the correct label, (4) kicks off a background learning cycle, and (5) stores a "memory" so a similar item auto-corrects on your next scan. All of this is inside RackTrack; none of it reaches the hardware.

entries.question: Does my correction help the model get better?
entries.answer: Yes — that's a core purpose. Each correction is saved as training data and feeds an active-learning cycle, and a memory of it is stored so visually similar devices, ports, or cables on future scans can auto-apply your label right away, even before a retrain.

entries.question: Do I have to correct things, or can I just confirm?
entries.answer: You can just confirm. Tapping Yes on the device and port-count cards records that the model's guess was right — that's useful signal too, and it feeds the accuracy score. Only tap No when something is actually wrong.

entries.question: If I tap "Yes," does anything get sent?
entries.answer: For the device and port-count cards, yes — a "correct" answer is recorded on the server. For the port-type card, tapping Yes is local only (nothing is sent); only a changed port type is submitted.

entries.question: Can I correct the port type of a jack?
entries.answer: Yes, after you locate a port. The card "Port type: X — right?" lets you set it to one of RJ45, SFP, QSFP, CONSOLE, AUX, MANAGEMENT_PORT, USB_A, USB_B, or USB_C. Saving it trains the type model and is remembered for re-scans of that port.

entries.question: Can I fix the port number or the cable colour too?
entries.answer: Yes. When you've located a port, RackTrack asks "Port \<n\> — right?" and "Cable colour is \<colour\> — right?". Correcting the number re-anchors that port and shifts the device's numbering to match; correcting the colour updates that cable. Both corrections are saved right from that on-screen prompt and take effect straight away.
entries.short: Yes — confirm or correct a port number or cable colour from the on-screen prompt; both save instantly.

entries.question: Where do my corrections show up?
entries.answer: Everywhere the scan is read — the Results UI, the device picker, Recent Scans, exported reports, and any ServiceNow sync. RackTrack rebuilds the canonical scan result with your corrections overlaid, so all consumers see the same corrected values.

entries.question: If I correct the same thing twice, do the corrections stack?
entries.answer: No. The most recent correction always wins. Port-number shifts, for example, are stored as absolute offsets so repeated corrections can't compound into a runaway shift — the latest one simply replaces the previous.

entries.question: Is my original detection lost when I correct it?
entries.answer: No. RackTrack keeps the model's original value (e.g. class_name_original) and a small _correction audit trail alongside the new value, so the original prediction is always recoverable.

entries.question: Who can make corrections?
entries.answer: Any signed-in user who can open that scan. Making corrections requires you to be signed in, and RackTrack checks that your organisation owns the rack — if it doesn't, the request is refused as "not found." The Ground Truth worklist screens are owner-only, but the device correction it submits is the same one available on any scan you can view.
entries.short: Any signed-in user who can open the scan; only your organisation's own racks can be corrected.

entries.question: Do corrections work across my whole organisation?
entries.answer: The learned memory is scoped to your organisation, so your corrections improve your organisation's future scans. The record change applies to the specific scan you corrected.

entries.question: Why did the device image change after I fixed the port count?
entries.answer: Because RackTrack redrew that device's port view to match your count — placing a dot and an index for every port. It's a fresh drawing of RackTrack's record, not a change to the switch.

entries.question: The count re-layout put ports in two rows — why?
entries.answer: RackTrack uses two rows when your count is even and the device face is short and wide (a typical rack switch), and a single row otherwise (patch panels, small devices). It numbers two-row switches column-by-column and single rows left to right, matching the app's normal switch numbering.

entries.question: What if the automatic re-layout can't run?
entries.answer: RackTrack still records the real count you entered, so the port-number entry box is bounded to 1–N straight away. You just won't get the freshly redrawn grid until it can re-run.

entries.question: Does a wrong correction ever risk the hardware?
entries.answer: No. The worst outcome of a mistaken correction is a wrong note in RackTrack, which you can correct again. Because corrections never reach the equipment, there is no hardware risk in experimenting.

entries.question: Can I lock in a whole port layout I've verified?
entries.answer: Yes. RackTrack can save a fully verified port layout for a scan. After that, re-uploading the same or a visually similar image returns your verified layout and skips port detection entirely — and the scan shows a VERIFIED badge.
entries.short: Yes — save a verified port layout; matching re-uploads reuse it, skip detection, and show a VERIFIED badge.

entries.question: How is accuracy measured from my feedback?
entries.answer: RackTrack tallies right vs wrong answers across your feedback to produce an overall accuracy figure and a per-device-class breakdown, shown on the owner dashboard. Confirmed-correct "Yes" answers count as right; corrections count as wrong-then-fixed. (Port-type answers don't carry a right/wrong flag, so they help train the model but don't move this number.)
entries.short: Your Yes/correction answers are tallied into an overall and per-device-class accuracy on the owner dashboard.

entries.question: Does correcting stuff slow the app down?
entries.answer: No. The learning and memory work runs in the background in separate processes, and the accuracy tally is cached, so your correction returns immediately while the heavier work happens out of the way.

entries.question: How do I start?
entries.answer: Get your invitation (or web link) from whoever runs RackTrack for your team, open the app, sign in, and press Start a scan. If you do not have an account yet, see Section 4.

entries.question: How do I start the app?
entries.answer: On an iPhone or iPad, tap the RackTrack icon that TestFlight installed. On Android, tap the RackTrack icon that Firebase App Distribution installed. On a computer, open the web link in your browser. Then sign in — RackTrack always opens on the home screen, and the main button takes you from there.

entries.question: How do I get RackTrack?
entries.answer: By invitation, not from an app store. For iPhone/iPad you are invited through TestFlight; for Android, through Firebase App Distribution; for a computer, you are simply given a web link. It is not listed in the public App Store or Play Store, so searching there will not find it. Ask your team's RackTrack administrator for an invitation.

entries.question: How do I run my first scan?
entries.answer: Sign in, press Start a scan, choose Upload or Camera, pick or take a photo of the rack, and press Analyze Rack. A few seconds later you land on the results. Section 6 has the full walkthrough.

entries.question: Why do I need to log in?
entries.answer: RackTrack has no guest mode — every feature that does real work sits behind the sign-in screen, and your scans belong to your account and your organization. Signing in is also what keeps each company's data private and shows you only the features your role allows.

entries.question: What can I do in RackTrack?
entries.short: At its core, you photograph a rack and get back a labelled inventory of its devices and ports, then explore views like Ports, Topology, Network, and Switches.
entries.answer: At its core, you photograph a rack and get back a labelled inventory of its devices and ports, then explore views like Ports, Topology, Network, and Switches. You can also scan two racks together to see the cabling between them, revisit your past scans, ask the built-in Ask DOT assistant for help, and contact support. Owners and admins can additionally manage their organization and members, connect outside systems, and use the Marketplace.

entries.question: Do I need to download anything from the App Store or Play Store?
entries.answer: No. RackTrack is not published in either public store. You install it from a tester invitation (TestFlight on Apple devices, Firebase App Distribution on Android) or just open the web link in a browser.

entries.question: Can I use RackTrack in a normal web browser?
entries.answer: Yes. It runs as a full website on a computer with nothing to install — open the web link and sign in. This is also a handy fallback if the installed app ever has trouble reaching the server.

entries.question: Do I need an account, or can I try it first?
entries.answer: You need an account; there is no try-before-you-sign-in mode. You get an account either by creating a new organization or by accepting an invitation.

entries.question: What is the difference between "Create an organization" and using an invite code?
entries.answer: Creating an organization makes a brand-new private space for your company, with you as its first member — and it waits for the platform owner's approval before switching on. An invite link joins you to an organization that already exists, with your role and site already set, and it lets you in immediately with no waiting.

entries.question: I created an organization but can't get past the "Waiting for approval" screen — is something broken?
entries.answer: No. New organizations are reviewed and approved by the platform owner before they go live. The screen checks automatically and lets you in the instant you are approved; you do not need to sign in again.

entries.question: My invite link doesn't work — what now?
entries.answer: Invites are single-use and can expire. Ask your organization's admin to send a new one. You cannot join an existing organization by signing yourself up.

entries.question: I forgot my password. How do I get back in?
entries.answer: On the sign-in screen tap Forgot password?, enter your email, and type the six-digit code that is emailed to you (it only lasts about a minute, so be quick, and use Resend if needed). You can then set a new password or simply choose to go straight into the app.

entries.question: Where did my scan go / how do I see past scans?
entries.answer: Open Profile (in the bottom bar or the sidebar), which keeps your account details and your history of scans. Every scan you run is saved there automatically.

entries.question: Do I need internet to use it?
entries.short: Yes, for the important parts. Signing in and analysing a photo both need the app to reach the RackTrack server, so a working connection is required. If the installed app cannot connect but you need in urgently, the web link on a connected device is your fallback.
entries.answer:
Yes, for the important parts. Signing in and analysing a photo both need the app to reach the RackTrack server, so a working connection is required. If the installed app cannot connect but you need in urgently, the web link on a connected device is your fallback.

---

— Getting Started with RackTrack —

entries.question: What is a U?
entries.answer: "U" is the standard unit of rack height — one U equals 1.75 inches (44.45 mm) of vertical space. Equipment is measured in U (a thin switch is 1U, a big server might be 2U or 4U), and RackTrack maps each device to the U slot(s) it occupies.

entries.question: What is a rack unit?
entries.answer: It's the same thing as a "U" (sometimes written "RU") — one 1.75-inch slot of vertical space in a rack. RackTrack builds an invisible ruler of these slots up the rack, numbered from the bottom (u01) upward, and assigns each device its slot.

entries.question: What is a U-position?
entries.answer: It's where a device sits on the rack ruler, given as a U number or range like "U05–U06." RackTrack numbers from the bottom up (u01 at the bottom) and uses the U-position to match scanned devices to CMDB records by position and type.

entries.question: What is a rack?
entries.answer: A standard 19-inch-wide metal frame that holds network and computer gear stacked vertically. RackTrack works one rack at a time: you photograph the front of a rack and it maps out what's inside.

entries.question: What is RJ45?
entries.answer: RJ45 is the common 8-pin copper connector on the end of an ordinary Ethernet cable, and the square jack it plugs into. In RackTrack, RJ45 ports are the "main" category, and a device's headline port count is its RJ45 count.

entries.question: What is SFP?
entries.answer: SFP is a small slot ("cage") on a switch that takes a plug-in transceiver module, usually for a fibre-optic or high-speed direct-attach cable. SFP+ is the same cage running at 10 Gbps. RackTrack detects the SFP cage from the photo and shows it under the SFP category.

entries.question: What is QSFP?
entries.answer: QSFP is a larger, four-channel transceiver cage used for high-speed uplinks (typically 40/100 Gbps). RackTrack detects it as its own port type but groups it under the same SFP category button as SFP.

entries.question: What is a console port?
entries.answer: A management socket used to connect directly to a device to configure it, separate from its data ports. RackTrack folds CONSOLE, AUX, and MANAGEMENT_PORT detections into one "Console" category.

entries.question: What is a patch panel?
entries.answer: A passive panel of many identical jacks (usually 24 or 48 RJ45 sockets) used to organise and terminate cabling — no power, no intelligence. RackTrack counts its jacks and snaps the total to the nearest standard size (24 or 48); because it's passive with no MAC address, it never appears in the live Network View.

entries.question: What is PoE?
entries.answer: Power over Ethernet — a switch sending electrical power down the same Ethernet cable that carries data, so a camera, phone, or access point needs only one cable. RackTrack shows a switch's PoE budget (in watts) on the live Ports/Lab view when the switch reports it over SSH.

entries.question: What is a UPS?
entries.answer: An Uninterruptible Power Supply — a battery-backed unit that keeps equipment running through a power cut and smooths out spikes. RackTrack detects it as one of its 12 device classes; it's placed in the rack inventory but has no network ports to inspect.

entries.question: What is a switch?
entries.answer: A network device that connects many wired devices and forwards traffic between them, usually a flat 1U/2U box with a row of ports. It's central to RackTrack: their standard 1U height sets the rack ruler, and Switch Information, Network View, and the live Ports tab all work on switches.

entries.question: What is a router?
entries.answer: A device that moves traffic between separate networks (for example your office and the internet). RackTrack keeps Router as its own class, distinct from Switch, so it's never mislabelled as one.

entries.question: What is a firewall?
entries.answer: A security device that inspects traffic and allows or blocks it by rules, guarding the boundary between networks. RackTrack detects it as one of its port-bearing device classes.

entries.question: What is a gateway?
entries.answer: A device that serves as the entry/exit point between one network and another, often translating between systems. RackTrack treats it as its own port-bearing device class.

entries.question: What is a server?
entries.answer: A computer that runs applications, stores data, or serves other machines; in a rack it's a flat chassis one or more U tall. RackTrack detects servers but deliberately doesn't look for ports on them, to avoid inventing ports that aren't there.

entries.question: What is an uplink?
entries.answer: The connection that carries traffic out of a switch or rack up to a higher point — a core/aggregation switch or another rack. RackTrack draws switch uplinks fanning up to an external "UPLINK / CORE" point outside the rack, and in a two-rack scan it draws the inter-rack uplink cables crossing between the racks.

entries.question: What is a MAC address?
entries.answer: The unique hardware ID burned into every network interface, written as six hex pairs like 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E. Switches learn which MACs are reachable behind each port; RackTrack's Network View shows a per-port count of learned MACs so you can see how many devices are live behind a port.

entries.question: What is a VLAN?
entries.answer: A Virtual LAN — a way to split one physical switch into several separate logical networks, each with its own number, so ports on the same box act as if isolated. RackTrack groups a switch's live ports by VLAN in Network View. (It does not track VLAN changes as drift.)

entries.question: What is LLDP?
entries.answer: Link Layer Discovery Protocol — a vendor-neutral way for switches to announce themselves to directly-connected neighbours, so each end learns what's across a cable. RackTrack polls LLDP over SSH to read each port's neighbour, and a change of neighbour is how it flags a re-cabling.

entries.question: What is CDP?
entries.answer: Cisco Discovery Protocol — Cisco's own version of LLDP, and the default on Cisco IOS gear (which doesn't run LLDP unless told to). RackTrack asks for both LLDP and CDP and merges them, so the Neighbour column still fills in when LLDP is empty.

entries.question: What is a neighbour?
entries.answer: The device on the far end of a cable, discovered via LLDP or CDP. RackTrack shows it per port and in a Neighbours tab; if a port sees several neighbours (a shared segment), the extras show as a muted "+2".

entries.question: What is firmware?
entries.answer: The built-in software that runs a piece of hardware; keeping it current brings fixes and security patches. RackTrack reads a switch's firmware version from its faceplate (OCR), then Switch Information checks it against the vendor's latest and says "Up to date" or "Upgrade available" — it never invents a version.

entries.question: What is CMDB?
entries.answer: A Configuration Management Database — your system of record for what equipment exists and where, which in practice almost always means ServiceNow. RackTrack connects to it to register scanned racks into it and to reconcile it against what the camera actually sees.

entries.question: What is reconciliation?
entries.answer: Comparing what your CMDB expects in a rack against what the scan actually detected, one U-position at a time, and flagging every disagreement. RackTrack returns a verdict per record — match, low-confidence match, mismatch (physical drift), or unknown — matching by position and type, and posts the result as a work note on the ServiceNow incident.

entries.question: What is drift?
entries.answer: Its main sense is a recorded difference in a monitored switch's port state since the last poll — a link up/down, a speed change, a description edit, or a changed LLDP neighbour (a re-cable). Drift is a change log, not an alarm: it's stored and logged but never pushed as a notification. (Separately, "physical drift" means a device found at a different U than the CMDB expects.)

entries.question: What is ground truth?
entries.answer: An owner-only screen for verifying, device by device, what the model detected in a single scan — tapping "Correct" or "Not this" and picking the real type. Confirmations measure accuracy; corrections fix the label everywhere and become training examples. The term comes from machine learning, where "ground truth" is the known-correct answer a model is measured against.

entries.question: What is a segmentation model?
entries.answer: The AI model that finds the equipment in a rack photo — RackTrack's devices_seg.pt, a YOLOv8m-seg model trained on 12 device classes. "Segmentation" means it can outline each object's exact pixels, though RackTrack uses only its bounding boxes. It's the first and most important model in the pipeline.

entries.question: What does occlusion mean?
entries.answer: Occlusion is when the rack or its ports are hidden behind clutter, usually a dense bundle of cables. On upload, RackTrack's occlusion gate (a MobileNetV2 model) judges the photo clear-vs-occluded and hard-stops at a high score, offering side-angle re-capture — because a buried rack can hide devices, and warning you is more honest than quietly missing them.

entries.question: What is a bounding box?
entries.answer: The rectangle a detection model draws around something it found — one per device, one per port. RackTrack keys everything off these boxes: device boxes build the U-grid and the crops, port boxes drive counting and location.

entries.question: What is an overlay?
entries.answer: The annotated rack image with boxes and labels drawn on the photo, so you can see what RackTrack saw. The main overlays are the device overlay (device boxes with U labels) and the all-ports overlay (every device plus every detected port, colour-coded).

entries.question: What is OCR?
entries.answer: Optical Character Recognition — reading printed text out of an image. RackTrack runs OCR on each switch's faceplate to pull the maker, model, and firmware version, which drive Switch Information's lookups and can correct the port count against a known model's datasheet.

entries.question: What is confidence?
entries.answer: How sure a model is about one answer, shown as a percentage and a coloured chip — green when fairly sure (75%+), amber in the middle (50–74%), red when unsure (below 50%). Reconciliation uses a 0.5 threshold to separate a clean match from a low-confidence one.

entries.question: What is a scan?
entries.answer: One capture-and-analysis run on a rack: you give RackTrack a photo or video frame and it produces the full device-and-port inventory. Everything else — Results, Ports, Ground Truth, Drift, Reconciliation — operates on a scan, and each has a rack ID like RK-….

entries.question: What does "Unidentified" mean on my results?
entries.answer: It's a row the model saw as occupied but couldn't confidently name, or a port-bearing device demoted because no ports were found on it. It's kept visible on purpose — it's the most valuable thing for a person to correct — and it's the one placeholder that does appear in Ground Truth so an owner can give it a real type.

entries.question: What's the difference between "Empty" and "Closed Unit"?
entries.answer: Both are placeholders for rack slots with no real equipment: "Empty" is an open, unused gap, and "Closed Unit" is a slot covered by a blank filler panel. Neither is a real device, so both are hidden from the device picker, the port overlay, and Ground Truth.

entries.question: What is Ask DOT?
entries.answer: RackTrack's in-app support assistant (also called "Assist"). It answers only from a verified knowledge base and never makes things up — either word-for-word, or by rephrasing matched entries — and if nothing matches it honestly refuses and points you to support@racktrack.ai. Each answer carries a badge showing how it was produced.

entries.question: What is a two-rack scan (rack group)?
entries.answer: A capture of two racks together as one linked pair, from two photos or one panning video. Each rack is analysed as a normal single-rack scan; the group adds a combined view that draws the uplink cables crossing between the two racks. A group is identified by an ID like GRP-….

entries.question: What is ServiceNow, and why does it matter to RackTrack?
entries.short: ServiceNow is the IT-service-management and CMDB platform RackTrack integrates with most deeply — the one connection type where live registration, reconciliation, and incident refresh actually run. Every registration into it is gated behind a Service Request that must be approved before anything is written.

entries.question: How do I open it?
entries.answer: Scan and analyse a rack, open that rack's results, and choose Ground Truth from the rack's sub-navigation. It always opens against the specific scan you came from.

entries.question: Why don't I see the empty or closed rack slots?
entries.answer: Because they aren't equipment. A rack scan produces a row for every rack unit, including blank ones, which come through as "Empty" or "Closed Unit." There is nothing to verify about an empty slot, so Ground Truth hides those rows and shows you only real devices — exactly as the Results view does.

entries.question: Then why do I still see "Unidentified" devices?
entries.answer: Those are real devices the model saw but couldn't classify. They are the most valuable thing to verify, because a human can give them a name the model couldn't. Ground Truth keeps them deliberately.

entries.question: What happens when I press "Correct"?
entries.answer: It records that the model's guess was right for that device. It adds a confirmation to the feedback log but does not change the device's stored type — there is nothing to change.

entries.question: What happens when I press "Not this"?
entries.answer: You pick the real device type and press Save truth. That fixes the device's type in the scan (so it shows correctly everywhere the scan is re-opened), records the correction, saves the device's image crop, and feeds that labelled example into the model's active-learning memory.

entries.question: Will my correction change what the results screen shows?
entries.answer: Yes. A correction rewrites the device's class in the scan's stored data, so re-opening the scan — and the Recent Scans and pickers — reflects your corrected type. The original guess is preserved underneath as a record.

entries.question: Can I change my mind after answering?
entries.answer: Yes. Each verified row has a Change link that reopens the control. The feedback log keeps every answer, and the most recent one for a device wins.

entries.question: Is the page showing me a real photo of each device?
entries.answer: The page shows the whole annotated scan image at the top and text rows (position, type, confidence) for each device. RackTrack does produce a tight per-device crop under the hood — used for training and available through a crop endpoint — but the per-scan verification page itself displays the full rack image rather than a separate close-up per row.

entries.question: Does confirming a device improve the model?
entries.answer: Confirmations improve the measured accuracy — they tell us how often the model was right. It is corrections that produce new training examples. Both matter: one tells us how we're doing, the other makes us better.

entries.question: Where does my answer actually go?
entries.answer: Into the same device-feedback pipeline the Results screen uses: an append-only feedback.jsonl (both global and per-rack), the scan's stored device map (on corrections), and the active-learning memory (on corrections). It's a proven path, not a new one built just for Ground Truth.

entries.question: Could Ground Truth be opened to members later?
entries.short: It's built so it could be. The rack-visibility logic on the server already scopes results by role, so opening it up would mainly be a matter of relaxing the owner gates — but as verified today, it is strictly owner-only.
entries.answer:
It's built so it could be. The rack-visibility logic on the server already scopes results by role, so opening it up would mainly be a matter of relaxing the owner gates — but as verified today, it is strictly owner-only.

---

— Ground Truth —

entries.question: Why are the Link, Speed, Duplex or PoE columns blank?
entries.short: Because the switch genuinely reported nothing for them, and RackTrack shows the truth rather than guessing.
entries.answer: Because the switch genuinely reported nothing for them, and RackTrack shows the truth rather than guessing. PoE is always blank on the lab switches (virtual IOL has no PoE hardware). Link/Speed/Duplex/Type are blank on the L3 core's routed interfaces, because show interfaces status only lists Layer-2 switchports. Speed/Duplex can also be blank on the L2 switches because virtual IOL never negotiates a real physical link. A blank cell is "—" and means "nothing to report here."

entries.question: Does RackTrack change my switches when I open the Lab?
entries.answer: No. Never. Both the on-demand audit and the background poller run only read (show) commands plus session setup. RackTrack reads switches; it does not configure them, reboot them, or touch a port. The only script that writes to the lab switches (configure-lab.js) is a separate, hand-run setup tool that is not part of the app.

entries.question: Who can see the Lab?
entries.answer: Platform owners only. Both the device list and the audit endpoint are owner-restricted. Everyone else sees "Restricted to platform owners."

entries.question: Why did it show me old data first, then change?
entries.answer: By design. Logging into a switch takes a few seconds, so the page shows the last saved report instantly (stamped with its age) and then refreshes it live in the background. The report updates in place when the fresh read returns. You're never left waiting on a blank screen.

entries.question: How fresh is the report?
entries.answer: The line above the tabs tells you — "Audit as of 2m ago," or "Refreshing…" while a live read is running. The audit is a live SSH pass, not the background poll. Press Refresh audit any time to force a fresh read now.

entries.question: What's the difference between "Live," "Offline," "No data" and "Disabled" on a switch?
entries.answer: Live = reached and returning data. Offline = the last poll failed; the switch isn't answering. No data = never successfully reached yet (often missing credentials). Disabled = polling is turned off for that switch, so its data goes stale on purpose.

entries.question: A switch says Offline — what do I do?
entries.answer: Usually nothing on RackTrack's side. These are EVE-NG nodes whose config is volatile, so Offline almost always means the node is stopped or came back unconfigured. Start/reconfigure it in EVE-NG and polling recovers by itself. If you want to confirm the moment it's back, press Refresh audit — a successful read clears the Offline state immediately.

entries.question: Why doesn't it just poll every few seconds so it's always fresh?
entries.answer: Because these switches allow only one SSH session and hold it open even after the connection drops. Polling constantly would keep that single session permanently busy and starve your manual audits — and a burst of retries can wedge the switch. Hourly polling leaves the session free for the interactive reads that need it.

entries.question: Why can't I run two audits at once, or why does it feel like it "waits"?
entries.answer: The switch permits a single SSH session, so RackTrack serialises access: an audit tells the background poller to step aside, and the page auto-audits a switch only once per visit. This is intentional, to protect the switch from session exhaustion.

entries.question: Why is the Neighbour column populated by CDP sometimes?
entries.answer: The lab's IOL images often don't support LLDP, so show lldp neighbors detail comes back empty even though the ports are cabled. The audit also asks for CDP (Cisco's native neighbour protocol) and merges it in, which is why neighbours still appear.

entries.question: What does the "+2" next to a neighbour mean?
entries.answer: That local port saw more than one device (some lab ports share a single virtual segment). The first device is named and the muted "+2" tells you two more were seen — so a shared link isn't mistaken for a point-to-point one. The Neighbours tab lists them all individually.

entries.question: Where do the switch passwords live? Does my browser send them?
entries.answer: Neither the passwords nor even the switch's IP are ever sent by your browser — it sends only a device id. The server resolves the host and credentials from an encrypted store (keyed by vendor, with optional per-host overrides). No passwords are stored in the code.

entries.question: Who is allowed to use the Marketplace?
entries.answer: Only members whose role is Organization Admin or Owner. Any other member who opens a marketplace link is redirected to the home screen, and the server rejects the request as well. This is stricter than most RackTrack features.

entries.question: Do I need to be signed in just to look around?
entries.answer: Yes. Unlike a public shop, browsing here requires an admin/owner login — a signed-out visitor is sent to the login page first.

entries.question: What's the difference between "For sale" and "Wanted"?
entries.answer: "For sale" is gear you're offering; "Wanted" is a request describing something you need so sellers can find you and reach out. Only priced, active for-sale listings can be bought directly.

entries.question: How do I sell a device I just scanned?
entries.answer: Use the Sell action from a scan result. It opens the new-listing form pre-filled with the device's vendor, model, category and rack ID — the listing is then "scan-backed", which buyers can see.

entries.question: What is the 3% fee?
entries.answer: A flat platform fee added to the subtotal at checkout. The order summary shows the unit price, quantity, subtotal, the 3% fee and the total before you confirm.

entries.question: Do I have to pay through the app?
entries.answer: Only if this RackTrack server has Stripe configured — then you're redirected to Stripe to pay. If it isn't, the order is simply recorded and you arrange payment offline with the seller; the seller is told to ship once payment is confirmed.

entries.question: I left the price blank — can people still buy it?
entries.answer: No. A listing with no price reads "Make an offer" and has no Buy button; interested buyers are pointed to contact you directly.

entries.question: How do the buyer and seller talk to each other?
entries.answer: Every order carries a private message thread on the order page. It refreshes every 30 seconds, and either side can post (up to 2,000 characters a message).

entries.question: What do the order statuses mean?
entries.answer: Pending (awaiting payment), Paid (ready to ship), Shipped (on its way, with tracking), Completed (closed out by either party), Cancelled (stopped while still pending or paid).

entries.question: I can't delete a listing — why?
entries.answer: Because it already has one or more orders. To keep that history intact, deletion is blocked; mark the listing sold or closed instead.

entries.question: How do alerts find things for me?
entries.answer: Save a search — a label plus any of keyword, category, for-sale/wanted and a max price. Every new listing that matches all of your set filters drops into your Matches list, usually within minutes. You won't get alerted about your own listings, and you can keep up to 20 saved searches.

entries.question: Are the eBay, Amazon and FS.com links real listings on those sites?
entries.answer: No. They're just pre-filled searches that open in a new tab. RackTrack doesn't post anything on those sites through them and takes no cut — they're a convenience for looking further afield.

entries.question: What are Partner accounts for?
entries.answer: Connecting your own eBay or Amazon seller account (over OAuth, where the server has API keys) or a Discord channel (via webhook, which announces new listings). Discord works out of the box once you paste a webhook URL and can be tested with one button.

entries.question: What is the difference between "Two photos" and "One video"?
entries.answer: Two photos means you supply one photo per rack yourself. One video means you pan a single clip across both racks and RackTrack picks the best frame of each. Both end in the same place: two racks analysed and linked.

entries.question: Do I still get a full report for each rack?
entries.answer: Yes. Each rack in the pair is a complete, ordinary scan — same devices, ports, topology and report as if you had scanned it alone. Grouping only adds the pairing on top.

entries.question: Where did the Camera and Gallery buttons go?
entries.answer: They were replaced by a single tap-to-add box per rack. Tapping the box opens your phone's own chooser, which already offers "Take Photo" and "Photo Library," so there is nothing extra to press.

entries.question: Why is the "Build combined view" button greyed out?
entries.answer: It stays disabled until the current mode has what it needs — both photos in Two photos mode, or one clip in One video mode.

entries.question: What are the amber and blue cables in the combined view?
entries.answer: Those are the uplink cables that cross between the two racks. Amber is fibre, cyan/blue is direct-attach (DAC) copper. Cabling that stays inside a single rack is drawn separately, per rack.

entries.question: It says "Both photos resolved to the same rack." What went wrong?
entries.answer: The two photos are of the same rack (RackTrack recognises a rack by its image). It won't make a pair out of one rack — re-shoot so the two photos are of two different racks.

entries.question: My video only found one rack. Why?
entries.answer: The pan didn't clearly separate the two racks. Re-record slowly, giving each rack a clear moment on screen. Video mode needs at least two racks to build a pair.

entries.question: When I switch racks, why do I only see one rack at a time?
entries.answer: That is intentional. Showing one rack at a time keeps the page readable on a phone and, importantly, avoids running two live network probes at once on the Ports page. Switching racks cleanly resets that rack's page.

entries.question: I opened one of the racks later and the pairing was gone. Is that a bug?
entries.answer: No. The paired view only appears when you arrive with the group signal from the scan. Opening a single rack on its own deliberately shows just that rack — "you only get the report of what you uploaded."

entries.question: Can a rack be in more than one pair?
entries.answer: Yes. Because a rack is identified by its photo, the same rack can appear in several scans over time. When it matters, RackTrack resolves to the group you just created rather than an older one.

entries.question: How do I get to the between-rack 3D view?
entries.answer: From the results, tap the small 3D button next to the rack toggle. That opens the Combined topology, where both racks share one scene and the crossing cables are drawn and listed.

entries.question: Does this work if I'm not signed in?
entries.short: No. Multi-rack scans always belong to your tenant, so you need to be signed in — the video scan will refuse with "Authentication required" otherwise.
entries.answer:
No. Multi-rack scans always belong to your tenant, so you need to be signed in — the video scan will refuse with "Authentication required" otherwise.

---

Multi-Rack Scans (Two Racks) — RackTrack feature documentation.

entries.question: What is the difference between Network View and the rest of RackTrack?
entries.answer: Everywhere else, RackTrack works out connectivity from a photo. Network View reads it from the live network. It is the one view whose port state is verified, not inferred.

entries.question: It says "Network view is being prepared." Did I do something wrong?
entries.answer: No. That message means the discovery system is not reachable right now — often it is still warming up, or a scan is still syncing. It updates automatically from your scan; give it a moment and reopen.

entries.question: It says "No switches detected." Is that a bug?
entries.answer: Not necessarily. It means discovery is reachable but found no matching switches for this rack yet — normal for a rack with no network gear, or one whose switches have not been discovered. When one turns up, it appears here.

entries.question: What does the "N live" count mean?
entries.answer: It is how many of the rack's network devices were successfully matched to a live device in discovery. If the rack has ten switches but only six are on the network, you would see "6 live".

entries.question: Why is a device greyed out and marked "not in Network View"?
entries.answer: It means RackTrack could not match that scanned device to any live device — by management IP, by name, or by model. There is nothing live to expand, so the row is dimmed.

entries.question: Why don't I see patch panels?
entries.answer: Patch panels are passive — no MAC address, no agent — so they never show up as live neighbours on the network. Listing them would suggest a connection discovery cannot actually see, so they are left out.

entries.question: What do "up / total" and "links" mean on a device row?
entries.answer: "Up / total" is how many of the device's ports are up out of its total ports. "Links" is how many ports see something on the other end (a neighbour or a remote IP). The little bar visualises the up-percentage.

entries.question: The port shows "up (admin down)" on hover — what is that?
entries.answer: That is the fuller state label. The chip shows the operational state (up or down); the tooltip adds the administrative state when it differs — for example a port that is operationally up but administratively shut.

entries.question: I clicked the "N MAC" chip and nothing happened. Is it broken?
entries.answer: The chip does trigger a network-wide MAC lookup in the background, but the current page does not display the result, so nothing visibly changes. That is a limitation of the current screen, not a fault with your rack.

entries.question: Is there a button to sync a rack into Network View?
entries.answer: Not on the page today. Syncing happens automatically: after every scan (and again once the real make/model is read), the server pushes the rack into discovery for you. There is a manual sync endpoint on the server, but no button on the current screen calls it.

entries.question: How fresh is the data, and does the page keep refreshing?
entries.answer: Each device's ports are fetched the moment you expand it and then cached for that session, so re-opening is instant. It does not poll and auto-refresh on its own; reopening the device (or reloading the view) pulls it again.

entries.question: Is the data real or a demo?
entries.short: The page always shows whatever the discovery datastore holds. With a real polling network behind it, that is live truth. Right after a scan, the first values are seeded from the scan itself until polling refreshes them. In a demo without a real network, a seeded demonstration fabric can stand in — and real discovery replaces it once connected.
entries.answer: The page always shows whatever the discovery datastore holds. With a real polling network behind it, that is live truth. Right after a scan, the first values are seeded from the scan itself until polling refreshes them. In a demo without a real network, a seeded demonstration fabric can stand in — and real discovery replaces it once connected.

entries.question: Who is allowed to open the Operations Console?
entries.answer: Signed-in org admins and owners can open the page at /dashboard. But only owners — and any username the server has on its admin allow-list — actually see the data. An org admin who is not on that list will reach the page and see an "Owner access required" message instead of the dashboard.

entries.question: What is the difference between the Operations tab and the Logs tab?
entries.answer: The Operations tab shows what people did: a live trail of business actions (scans, sign-ins, feedback) drawn from the audit log. The Logs tab shows what the server did: its own runtime diary of web requests, email results and errors, drawn from the application log. Different records, different purposes.

entries.question: Does the page update on its own?
entries.answer: Yes. While the Live toggle is on, the Operations tab refreshes every 5 seconds and the Logs tab every 4 seconds. Only the tab you are viewing refreshes. Press Paused to stop it, or Refresh to force an immediate update. The relative times ("3m ago") also tick every second on their own.

entries.question: Why does someone show up as "anonymous" or "(no org)"?
entries.answer: Those rows are almost always leftovers from before login was required, so there is no account to attribute them to. Everything recorded now is tied to a real, named person. See section 8.

entries.question: What does "guest" or "not signed in" mean in the feed?
entries.answer: It marks an action that genuinely happened before a session existed — signing in, signing up, or resetting a password. The feed then shows the identifier the person typed rather than a stored name. It is expected behaviour.

entries.question: What exactly counts as a "scan" in these numbers?
entries.answer: A successfully recorded rack-scan action. "Scans today" and "Total scans" count those; the failed-scans figures count scan-family actions that failed.

entries.question: How is "Success rate" worked out?
entries.answer: It is the share of all recorded actions that succeeded — one minus (failed actions ÷ all actions). It is not limited to scans, so failed logins or other failures lower it too. It turns amber below 90%.

entries.question: Where does "Accuracy (feedback)" come from?
entries.answer: From the model-feedback answers people give in Ground Truth — right ÷ (right + wrong). It reads "no feedback yet" until any has been given, and turns amber below 80%. It is not part of the audit log.

entries.question: Can I find every log line that belongs to one web request?
entries.answer: Yes. Expand any log row to see its request id, then search for that id to pull every line RackTrack wrote while handling that single request.

entries.question: What does "Clear log" do, and can I undo it?
entries.answer: It permanently wipes the stored application log and starts fresh — it cannot be undone, so it asks you to confirm. It only clears the server's runtime log; it does not touch the audit trail or any business data, and the clear itself is recorded in the audit trail.

entries.question: How long are logs kept?
entries.answer: The application log keeps about 7 days by default and is capped at 200,000 rows, pruning itself as it goes — whichever limit is reached first wins. The retention window is shown on the count line ("kept N days"). The audit trail behind the Operations tab is a permanent record and is not pruned this way.

entries.question: Could a password or secret end up in the logs?
entries.answer: No. The application log mirrors the exact line the server has already redacted before writing it, so anything the logger hides stays hidden in this view too.

entries.question: Is the old `/logs` page gone?
entries.answer: The address still works but now redirects to /dashboard. The logs viewer is now the Logs tab inside the Operations Console rather than a separate page.

entries.question: Who can see my racks?
entries.answer: Only you, your organization's admin, and the platform owner. As a member you see just the racks you personally scanned; your org admin sees everything across your whole organization; the owner sees everything on the platform. Your teammates do not see your scans, and nobody in another organization can see them at all.

entries.question: Can another company ever see our data?
entries.answer: No. Every organization is walled off. There is no path — through the screen or underneath it — from one organization to another's racks, sites, or people.

entries.question: What exactly can an owner do?
entries.answer: Everything, everywhere. The owner creates organizations and their admins, approves or rejects sign-ups, renames, deactivates, or removes organizations, edits or removes anyone (including org admins), and sees every rack on the platform. The owner is also the only role that can manage an org admin.

entries.question: What's the difference between an org admin and a site manager?
entries.answer: An org admin runs the whole organization — all its sites, all its members, its shared integrations, and it sees every rack in the organization. A site manager looks after just one site: they can add and invite plain members to it and can toggle those members on/off or reset their passwords, but they cannot manage other managers, cannot reach other sites, and see only their own scans.

entries.question: Is there a role called "user"?
entries.answer: Not literally. The everyday user is a member. Above members sits site_manager, and above that org_admin, then owner. People often say "user" informally to mean a member.

entries.question: How do I get into RackTrack?
entries.answer: Two ways. Either found a new organization by signing up with your company name (which needs the platform owner's approval), or accept an invitation link from someone already in an organization (no approval, no waiting).

entries.question: Why is my new organization stuck on a waiting screen?
entries.answer: Because self-signed-up organizations start as a request and need the platform owner to approve them before they go live. The screen re-checks every few seconds and opens on its own the moment you are approved — you don't need to sign in again.

entries.question: Do invitations expire?
entries.answer: Yes. An invitation link works once and stops working after 7 days. If it lapses, ask your admin to generate a new one.

entries.question: If I invite someone, can they give themselves a higher role?
entries.answer: No. The role and site are baked into the invitation link. Whoever accepts it lands exactly where you set them, and cannot upgrade themselves. Admins and managers also can only ever hand out roles at or below their own level.

entries.question: What happens to someone's scans if I remove them?
entries.answer: The scans stay. Removing a member deletes the account but preserves their scan history; those scans simply show the scanner as "—" from then on. (You can't remove your own account.)

entries.question: What's the difference between deactivating and removing?
entries.answer: Deactivating is reversible — an off account keeps all its data and history but can't sign in until it's switched back on. Removing is permanent — it deletes the account (though, again, its past scans remain on the record).

entries.question: Are the scans and counts on the console real?
entries.answer: Yes. Everything shown — organizations, sites, members, invitations, and scans — is live, real data. And because scanning and giving feedback both require being signed in, every scan is attributed to a genuine, named person.

entries.question: Can a member or site manager open the organization console?
entries.short: No. The console is only for owners and org admins. Anyone else who reaches it is sent straight back to the app — administration is a role-scoped tool, and the roles that don't administer never see it.
entries.answer:
No. The console is only for owners and org admins. Anyone else who reaches it is sent straight back to the app — administration is a role-scoped tool, and the roles that don't administer never see it.

---

— Organizations, Roles & Access —

entries.question: What exactly does "drift" mean here?
entries.answer: A port is in a different state now than the last time the poller read it. It is a recorded difference — not an alarm, not necessarily a problem. The change log is simply the list of those differences over time.

entries.question: How often does it check the switch?
entries.answer: By default once an hour. It used to be once a minute, but that starved the switch's single SSH session, so the default was moved to hourly. You can always press Poll now for an immediate read.

entries.question: Will it alert me when something changes?
entries.answer: No. This is the key limitation: drift is stored and logged, never pushed. There is no email, popup, or notification. You have to open the Drift view to see it.

entries.question: Which fields count as a change?
entries.answer: Operational state, admin state, speed, duplex, flow control, medium, description, and the three LLDP neighbour fields (chassis, remote port, system name). A difference in any of those is recorded. Description tracking can be turned off with an env setting.

entries.question: Does it track VLAN changes?
entries.answer: No. Despite the tab's subtitle mentioning VLAN, VLAN is not a tracked field and is not stored — a VLAN change produces no drift event today.

entries.question: Why is my brand-new switch's history empty?
entries.answer: Because there is nothing to compare against yet. The first successful poll just sets the baseline. History fills in as the poller keeps running over the following hours; give it a few cycles.

entries.question: The screen says "runs once per minute" — is that right?
entries.answer: That empty-state text is stale. The real default is hourly. Trust the hourly cadence.

entries.question: What happens if the switch is offline or unreachable?
entries.answer: The poll fails, the device is backed off (starting around a minute and doubling up to 30 minutes), and it is retried later instead of every interval. Once it answers again, the backoff clears. Server restart also clears backoff so polling resumes immediately.

entries.question: Does opening the timeline or changing the window re-read the switch?
entries.answer: No. The grid, timeline, "value at" table and change log are all drawn from stored history. The switch is only contacted by the scheduled poller and by an explicit Poll now.

entries.question: Why do I see five identical rows collapsed into one in the "Value at" table?
entries.answer: Because snapshots are stored only on change, one stored reading can be the correct answer for several time windows at once. The UI collapses identical answers so you are not shown the same row five times.

entries.question: How does it catch someone moving a cable?
entries.answer: The port advertises its neighbour over LLDP. When that neighbour's system name changes, it is recorded as an lldp_system event, and the timeline draws the new neighbour in a different colour — a visible seam at the moment of the reroute.

entries.question: Which switches does this work fully on?
entries.short: TP-Link JetStream and Cisco IOS have exact parsers with full per-port detail. About fifty other vendors from the CLI matrix get a generic recipe that reads identity but does not produce a per-port grid or drift.
entries.answer:
TP-Link JetStream and Cisco IOS have exact parsers with full per-port detail. About fifty other vendors from the CLI matrix get a generic recipe that reads identity but does not produce a per-port grid or drift.

---

— Port History & Drift —

entries.question: Why does it say "we couldn't read how many ports this device has"?
entries.short: Because the CV models — which count ports by looking at the photo — returned zero for this device.
entries.answer: Because the CV models — which count ports by looking at the photo — returned zero for this device. That happens when the crop is too dark/blurry, the ports are hidden behind cables, the device genuinely has no RJ45 jacks, or the port models aren't loaded on the server. Rather than let you locate a port with no honest upper bound (and risk pointing at nothing), RackTrack asks you to set the real count first. Answer the port-count question below the input and Find Port will work.

entries.question: Does Port Locate log in to the switch?
entries.answer: No. Port Locate works entirely from the photo of the rack using CV models. The separate Ports tab is the one that logs in to the live switch over SSH for real-time free/used counts.

entries.question: Where does the port count come from, then?
entries.answer: Two CV models on the device crop: ports_9.pt reads each port's type, and port_count.pt reads each port's status (connected/empty). The RJ45 tally becomes the device's port_count; SFP, Console, and USB get their own separate counts.

entries.question: I set the count and now it works — did that change the switch?
entries.answer: No. Your correction updates RackTrack's record of that device (and re-lays-out its ports so the numbering matches), and it's saved as feedback. It never touches the real hardware.

entries.question: The port shows "empty" but I think a cable is plugged in — why?
entries.answer: The status model reads occupancy from the photo. If it genuinely couldn't measure that port, RackTrack shows it as empty on this screen as the cautious default (it won't claim a link it didn't see). The angle, lighting, or a dust cap can cause a miss. Trust the live Ports tab or the switch itself for a definitive answer.

entries.question: Why are there four port types but only RJ45/SFP on the other view?
entries.answer: Port Locate distinguishes four physical categories — RJ45, SFP, Console, USB — folded from nine detector classes. The live Ports tab is a different feature that only splits copper (ETH) from fibre (SFP), because that's what the switch's own interface table gives it.

entries.question: My device is all-fibre and shows 0 RJ45. Is that a bug?
entries.answer: No. The models only see connector shapes. A device with no copper jacks correctly has 0 RJ45 — its ports are under the SFP (and maybe Console) buttons. You'll only see the type buttons for categories the device actually has.

entries.question: Can I locate a second port without starting over?
entries.answer: Yes. After a result, a compact "another port" input lets you type a new number — and you can switch the port type there too — to locate a different port on the same device immediately.

entries.question: What are the two images I get?
entries.answer: A cropped close-up of just that device with the port circled, and the full rack photo with the same port highlighted — so you can find it both up close and in context.

entries.question: What happens to a port I locate — is it recorded?
entries.answer: Yes. Each locate appends an entry to the device's port-identification log and archives the two images, so the report can show every port you've inspected, not just the last one.

entries.question: Can I select a Server, PSU, or UPS?
entries.answer: No. Only port-bearing types are selectable — Switch, Patch Panel, Router, Gateway, Firewall, and PDU. Other detected gear still appears on the annotated image but has no port to point at.

entries.question: What if I pick a PDU?
entries.answer: You get a Power summary (outlets total / in use / free and a Powered badge) instead of a port-number input. PDU outlets are counted by a dedicated power-outlet detector, not the port models.

entries.question: Why won't it accept "port 34" on a 24-port switch?
entries.short: The input is capped at the device's detected (or your corrected) count, and Find Port validates against it. Out-of-range numbers, decimals, and signs are rejected — a guard added after an unbounded number once located a port that didn't exist.
entries.answer:
The input is capped at the device's detected (or your corrected) count, and Find Port validates against it. Out-of-range numbers, decimals, and signs are rejected — a guard added after an unbounded number once located a port that didn't exist.

---

Two models read the photo — one for what each port is, one for whether it's in use. When they can't count, RackTrack asks you rather than guess.

entries.question: Where do I find my past scans?
entries.answer: Open the Profile tab and look at the Recent Scans list. Everything you have scanned is there, newest first.

entries.question: There used to be a separate "Scan history" page — where did it go?
entries.answer: It has been folded into Profile. The old /history address now opens Profile automatically, and your history shows as the Recent Scans list.

entries.question: If I scan on my phone, will the scan show up on my tablet?
